items.q: Two identical conducting spheres, fixed in place, attract each other with a force of $0.108\,\mathrm{N}$ when their centres are $50.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart. They are then joined by a thin wire and the wire is removed; now they repel each other with a force of $0.0360\,\mathrm{N}$. The initial net charge is positive. What was the negative charge on one of the spheres?
items.explain:
Before: $q_1q_2=-\dfrac{Fr^2}{k}=-3.00\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2}$ (opposite signs).
After touching, identical spheres share the net charge equally: $\left(\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}\right)^2=\dfrac{F'r^2}{k}\Rightarrow q_1+q_2=2.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$ (positive).
So $q_1,q_2$ are the roots of $x^2-2.00\times10^{-6}x-3.00\times10^{-12}=0$: $x=+3.00\times10^{-6}$ and $-1.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q1(a)

items.q: For the two identical conducting spheres of the previous problem (attraction $0.108\,\mathrm{N}$ at $50.0\,\mathrm{cm}$; after contact repulsion $0.0360\,\mathrm{N}$; positive net charge), what was the POSITIVE charge on the other sphere?
items.explain: The two initial charges are the roots of $x^2-(q_1+q_2)x+q_1q_2=0$ with $q_1+q_2=2.00\times10^{-6}$ and $q_1q_2=-3.00\times10^{-12}$: $+3.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$ and $-1.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q1(b)

items.q: Four particles sit at the corners of a square. Particles 1 and 4 (on one diagonal) have charge $Q$; particles 2 and 3 (on the other diagonal) have charge $q$. What is $Q/q$ if the net electrostatic force on particles 1 and 4 is zero?
items.explain:
Force on particle 1 from its two neighbours (charge $q$, distance $a$) points along the sides: each has magnitude $\dfrac{kQq}{a^2}$, resultant $\sqrt2\,\dfrac{kQq}{a^2}$ along the diagonal.
The opposite corner (charge $Q$, distance $a\sqrt2$) pushes along the diagonal with $\dfrac{kQ^2}{2a^2}$. Balance: $\sqrt2\,Qq=-\dfrac{Q^2}{2}$, so $\dfrac Qq=-2\sqrt2=-2.83$.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q2(a)

items.q: In the same square (charges $Q$ on one diagonal, $q$ on the other), is there any value of $q$ (for fixed $Q$) that makes the net electrostatic force zero on ALL four particles?
opts: No: balance on particles 1, 4 needs $Q/q=-2\sqrt2$ but on 2, 3 it needs $Q/q=-1/(2\sqrt2)$
Yes, any $q$ with opposite sign to $Q$
items.explain: For particles 2 and 3 the roles are exchanged: zero force needs $q/Q=-2\sqrt2$, i.e. $Q/q=-1/(2\sqrt2)=-0.354$. The two conditions $-2.83$ and $-0.354$ contradict each other, so no value of $q$ works.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q2(b)

items.q: Particle 1 ($q_1=3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$) is at $(3.5\,\mathrm{cm},\,0.50\,\mathrm{cm})$ and particle 2 ($q_2=-4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$) at $(-2.0\,\mathrm{cm},\,1.5\,\mathrm{cm})$. What is the magnitude of the electrostatic force on particle 2 due to particle 1?
items.src: Homework session 1, Q3(a)

items.q: For the same two charges (particle 2 is attracted by particle 1), what is the direction of the force on particle 2, as an angle from the $+x$ axis?
items.explain:
The force on particle 2 points TOWARDS particle 1 (opposite charges attract): direction $(+5.5,\,-1.0)\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Angle $=\arctan\dfrac{-1.0}{5.5}=-10.3^\circ$, i.e. $10.3^\circ$ below the $+x$ axis.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q3(b)

items.q: A third particle with $q_3=+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ is to be placed so that the net force on particle 2 vanishes. Its coordinates (in cm) are
items.explain:
Particle 3 must pull particle 2 with the same $34.5\,\mathrm{N}$ in the OPPOSITE direction, so it lies on the line through 1 and 2, beyond 2 (away from 1).
Distance: $\dfrac{k|q_2q_3|}{r_3^2}=34.5\Rightarrow r_3=6.46\,\mathrm{cm}$ along the unit vector $(-5.5,\,1.0)/5.59$.
Position $=(-2.0,\,1.5)+6.46(-0.984,\,0.179)=(-8.35,\,2.66)\,\mathrm{cm}$.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q3(c, d)

items.q: Particle 1 (charge $q$) and particle 2 (charge $4.00q$) are held $9.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart on the $x$ axis. Where on the axis (distance from particle 1, in cm) must a third particle be placed so that it feels no net force?
items.explain:
Between the two charges the forces on a test charge balance when $\dfrac{q}{x^2}=\dfrac{4q}{(L-x)^2}\Rightarrow L-x=2x$.
$x=\dfrac L3=3.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ from particle 1 (closer to the smaller charge).
items.src: Homework session 1, Q4(a, b)

items.q: A third particle placed at $L/3$ from particle 1 (charge $q$; particle 2 has charge $4q$, $L=9.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart) must be such that ALL THREE particles stay in place when released. What is $q_3/q$?
items.explain:
Particle 1 is pushed away from particle 2 by $\dfrac{k(q)(4q)}{L^2}$, so particle 3 must pull it back: $\dfrac{k\,q|q_3|}{(L/3)^2}=\dfrac{4kq^2}{L^2}\Rightarrow|q_3|=\dfrac{4q}{9}$.
$q_3$ must be negative (attractive for particle 1): $q_3/q=-\dfrac49=-0.444$.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q4(c)

items.q: What is the magnitude of the electrostatic force between a singly charged sodium ion (charge $+e$) and an adjacent singly charged chlorine ion ($-e$) in a salt crystal if their separation is $2.82\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.src: Homework session 1, Q6

items.q: An electron and a positron have charges $-e$ and $+e$ and equal masses $9.11\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$. What is the ratio of the electrical force to the gravitational force between them?
items.explain:
Both forces fall off as $1/r^2$, so the distance cancels: $\dfrac{F_e}{F_g}=\dfrac{ke^2}{Gm^2}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{(6.674\times10^{-11})(9.11\times10^{-31})^2}=4.17\times10^{42}$.
Gravity is utterly negligible between elementary particles.
items.src: Homework session 1, Q7

items.explain: $F\propto1/r^2$: $r\to3r$ gives $F\to F/9$.

items.q: One of two point charges is doubled and the distance between them is also doubled. The force between them becomes
items.explain: $F\propto\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\to\dfrac{2}{4}F=\dfrac F2$.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (Coulomb's law)

items.q: Three point charges lie on the $x$ axis: $+3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ at $x=0$, $-2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ at $x=0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ and $+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ at $x=0.25\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the net force on the $-2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge (positive = towards $+x$)?
items.explain:
From the $+3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge (attraction, towards $-x$): $F=\dfrac{k(3.0)(2.0)\times10^{-12}}{0.10^2}=5.39\,\mathrm{N}$.
From the $+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge (attraction, towards $+x$, $r=0.15\,\mathrm{m}$): $\dfrac{k(4.0)(2.0)\times10^{-12}}{0.15^2}=3.20\,\mathrm{N}$.
Net $=-5.39+3.20=-2.19\,\mathrm{N}$, i.e. $2.19\,\mathrm{N}$ towards $-x$ (superposition: add vectors with signs).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q3

items.q: A $3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge sits at the origin. A $+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge is on the $x$ axis at $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ and a $+6.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge on the $y$ axis at $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the magnitude of the net force on the $3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge?
items.explain:
$F_x=\dfrac{k(3.0)(4.0)\times10^{-12}}{0.20^2}=2.70\,\mathrm{N}$ (pushing towards $-x$), $F_y=\dfrac{k(3.0)(6.0)\times10^{-12}}{0.30^2}=1.80\,\mathrm{N}$ (towards $-y$).
The forces are perpendicular: $F=\sqrt{2.70^2+1.80^2}=3.24\,\mathrm{N}$ (not the sum $4.5\,\mathrm{N}$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q3

items.q: Two identical small conducting spheres carry charges 6 μC and -2 μC. They are touched together and separated. What is the charge on each sphere afterwards (in μC)?
items.explain: Identical conductors share the total charge equally (charge is conserved): $q=\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}=\dfrac{6+(-2)}{2}=2\,\mu\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q1

items.q: Two identical small conducting spheres carry charges 9 μC and 3 μC. They are touched together and separated. What is the charge on each sphere afterwards (in μC)?
items.explain: Identical conductors share the total charge equally (charge is conserved): $q=\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}=\dfrac{9+(3)}{2}=6\,\mu\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q1

items.q: Two identical small conducting spheres carry charges -8 μC and 2 μC. They are touched together and separated. What is the charge on each sphere afterwards (in μC)?
items.explain: Identical conductors share the total charge equally (charge is conserved): $q=\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}=\dfrac{-8+(2)}{2}=-3\,\mu\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q1

items.q: How many excess electrons are on an object carrying a charge of $-1.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$?
items.explain: Charge is quantised, $q=ne$: $n=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-6}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=6.2\times10^{12}$ electrons.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (charge is quantised)

items.q: In a hydrogen atom the electron is on average $5.29\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m}$ from the proton. What is the electrostatic force between them?
items.explain: $F=\dfrac{ke^2}{r^2}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{(5.29\times10^{-11})^2}=8.2\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{N}$: tiny, yet it acts on a mass of only $9\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q6

items.q: Two metal spheres, one positively charged and one neutral, are brought into contact and separated. The neutral sphere ends up
opts: positively charged (electrons moved from it to the other sphere)
items.explain: Electrons (the mobile carriers) flow from the neutral sphere to the positive one until their potentials equalise; the neutral sphere is left with a deficit of electrons, i.e. positive. Protons do not move in a conductor.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (charge transfer)

items.q: A negatively charged rod is brought near, but does not touch, a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand; the sphere is briefly grounded (touched by a finger) with the rod still in place, and then the rod is removed. The sphere is
opts: positively charged only on its far side
items.explain: Charging by induction: the rod repels electrons from the sphere to the ground. Removing the ground connection first and the rod afterwards leaves the sphere with a net positive charge, spread uniformly over the surface.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (charging by induction)

items.q: Which statement describes the conservation of charge correctly?
opts: The net charge of an isolated system never changes
Positive charge is always conserved but negative is not
Charge is conserved only in collisions of particles
Charge can be created from energy
items.explain: Charge can be transferred, and particle-antiparticle pairs can be created with total charge zero, but the algebraic sum of the charges of an isolated system is constant.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (conservation of charge)

items.q: A charged particle is inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell. The net electrostatic force on it from the shell is
opts: directed towards the nearest part of the shell
the same as if the shell's charge were at its centre
items.explain: Shell theorem 2: inside a uniformly charged shell the forces from all parts cancel. Outside, the shell acts like a point charge at its centre (shell theorem 1).
items.src: Midterm tutoring slides (shell theories)

items.q: A thin spherical shell of radius $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a uniformly distributed charge of $+8.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$. What force does it exert on a point charge of $+1.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ at $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ from its centre?
items.explain: Outside a uniformly charged shell the force is that of a point charge at the centre: $F=\dfrac{k(8.0\times10^{-6})(1.0\times10^{-6})}{0.50^2}=0.288\,\mathrm{N}$ (repulsive). Do not measure the distance to the surface.
items.src: Midterm tutoring slides (shell theories)

items.q: How large is the electrostatic repulsion between two protons that are $4.0\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$ apart inside a nucleus?
items.explain: $F=\dfrac{ke^2}{r^2}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{(4.0\times10^{-15})^2}=14\,\mathrm{N}$: enormous for a proton, and held in check by the strong nuclear force.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (Coulomb's law), charge is quantised

items.q: What is the total charge of one mole of electrons ($N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$)?
items.explain: $Q=N_Ae=(6.022\times10^{23})(1.602\times10^{-19})=9.65\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{C}$ (the Faraday constant).
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (Coulomb's law), charge is quantised

items.q: In the nuclear decay $^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}\to{}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{Rn}+{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$, charge conservation fixes the atomic number $Z$ of the radon nucleus to be
items.explain: Charge (atomic number) is conserved: $88=Z+2\Rightarrow Z=86$ (the mass number gives $A=226-4=222$).
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (Coulomb's law), charge is conserved

items.q: In the decay of a free neutron, $n\to p+e^-+\bar\nu$, which fact about charge is illustrated?
opts: the net charge before ($0$) equals the net charge after ($+e-e+0$)
charge is created in the decay
items.explain: Charges $0\to(+e)+(-e)+0=0$: charged particles appear in pairs, the total stays constant.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (Coulomb's law), charge is conserved

items.q: Three equal charges of $3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the magnitude of the net force on one of them?
items.explain:
Each of the other two charges pushes with $F_0=\dfrac{kq^2}{a^2}=0.324\,\mathrm{N}$, at $60^\circ$ to each other.
Resultant $=2F_0\cos30^\circ=\sqrt3\,F_0=0.561\,\mathrm{N}$ along the bisector, away from the other two.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q2

items.q: Four equal charges of $2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ are at the corners of a square of side $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the magnitude of the net force on one charge?
items.explain:
Let $F_0=\dfrac{kq^2}{a^2}=0.400\,\mathrm{N}$. The two neighbours give $F_0$ each at $90^\circ$: resultant $\sqrt2F_0$ along the diagonal.
The opposite corner (distance $a\sqrt2$) adds $\dfrac{F_0}{2}$ in the same direction. Net $=\left(\sqrt2+\tfrac12\right)F_0=0.765\,\mathrm{N}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q2

items.q: At what separation is the electrostatic repulsion between two $1.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charges equal to the weight of a $1.0\,\mathrm{g}$ mass?
items.explain: $\dfrac{kq^2}{r^2}=mg\Rightarrow r=q\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{mg}}=10^{-6}\sqrt{\dfrac{8.99\times10^9}{(10^{-3})(9.8)}}=0.96\,\mathrm{m}$: electrical forces on everyday objects are huge compared with gravity.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q7

items.q: Two charges $+9.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ and $+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ are $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ apart. At what point on the line between them (distance from the larger charge) is the force on a small test charge zero?
items.explain: Zero force when $\dfrac{9}{x^2}=\dfrac{4}{(0.50-x)^2}\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{0.50-x}=\dfrac32\Rightarrow x=0.30\,\mathrm{m}$ from the larger charge (nearer the smaller one).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q4

items.q: Coulomb's law $F=kq_1q_2/r^2$ applies directly to
opts: any two charged objects at any separation
point charges and, outside them, uniformly charged spheres
items.explain: It holds for point charges; by the shell theorem a uniformly charged sphere acts like a point charge at its centre for outside points. Extended objects need integration.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (Coulomb's law)

items.q: The electrostatic force between two charges acts
opts: perpendicular to the line joining them
along the line joining them, with equal magnitudes on the two charges
with a magnitude that depends on the direction of the line
items.explain: It is a central force obeying Newton's third law: equal and opposite on the two charges.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (Coulomb's law)

items.q: Rubbing a glass rod with silk makes the rod positive. This happens because
opts: charge is created on the rod
electrons move from the rod to the silk
protons move from the rod to the silk
electrons move from the silk to the rod
items.explain: Only electrons transfer between solids by friction. The rod loses electrons (net positive) and the silk gains them (net negative): the total charge stays zero.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C1 (charge transfer)

items.q: A material in which charges are NOT free to move is called
items.explain: In an insulator (non-conductor) the charges stay where they are put; in a conductor they move freely.
items.src: Midterm tutoring slides (conductors and insulators)

items.q: A $6.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ and a $2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge are $0.40\,\mathrm{m}$ apart. What is the force on the $2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge?
items.explain: $F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(6.0\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{-6})}{0.40^2}=0.674\,\mathrm{N}$. By Newton's third law the $6.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ charge feels exactly the same force (the bigger charge does not feel a bigger force).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q6

items.q: Two charges repel each other with a force of $0.20\,\mathrm{N}$ at a distance of $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the force at a distance of $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain: $F\propto1/r^2$: the distance is divided by $3$, so the force is multiplied by $9$: $1.8\,\mathrm{N}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q6

items.q: Sphere A has $+8.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ and an identical sphere B is neutral. A touches B, they are separated, then B touches a third identical neutral sphere C. What is the final charge on B (in $\mu$C)?
items.explain: A and B share: $+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ each. Then B and C share B's $+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ equally: B ends with $+2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ (and C with $+2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$, A keeps $+4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Q1

items.q: In a region the electric field lines on the left have twice the separation of those on the right. If the field magnitude at A (left) is $40\,\mathrm{N/C}$, what is the magnitude of the force on a proton at A?
items.src: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q1(a)

items.q: Field lines on the left of a figure are twice as far apart as the lines on the right. If the field is $40\,\mathrm{N/C}$ on the left (at A), what is the field magnitude on the right (at B)?
items.explain: The density of field lines (lines per unit area) is proportional to $E$. Lines twice as close means twice the density, so $E_B=2\times40=80\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
items.src: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q1(b)

items.q: Which statement about electric field lines is correct?
opts: They start on negative charges and end on positive charges
They start on positive charges, end on negative charges, and never cross
They can cross where the field is strongest
items.explain: The field is tangent to the line and points away from positive charges; the number of lines per unit area measures $E$. A crossing would mean two field directions at one point.
items.src: Midterm tutoring slides (mapping electric fields)

items.q: Charge is distributed uniformly around a ring of radius $R=2.40\,\mathrm{cm}$. At what distance from the ring's centre, along its axis, is the field magnitude greatest?
items.explain:
$E(z)=\dfrac{kQz}{(z^2+R^2)^{3/2}}$. Set $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}z}=0$: $(z^2+R^2)-3z^2=0\Rightarrow z=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt2}=1.70\,\mathrm{cm}$.
A numerical maximisation of $E(z)$ confirms $z=1.70\,\mathrm{cm}$ (zero at the centre, and decaying as $1/z^2$ far away).
items.src: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q4

items.q: A charge $q=7.81\,\mathrm{pC}$ is spread uniformly along a thin non-conducting rod of length $L=14.5\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is the magnitude of the electric field at point P, at distance $R=6.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the rod along its perpendicular bisector?
items.explain:
Integrate over the rod (the components along the rod cancel): $E=\dfrac{kq}{R\sqrt{R^2+(L/2)^2}}$.
$E=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(7.81\times10^{-12})}{(0.0600)\sqrt{0.0600^2+0.0725^2}}=12.4\,\mathrm{N/C}$, pointing away from the rod (for positive $q$). Numerical quadrature of the exact integral agrees; treating the rod as a point charge gives $19.5\,\mathrm{N/C}$, too much.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q5

items.q: At what distance along the central perpendicular axis of a uniformly charged plastic disk of radius $0.600\,\mathrm{m}$ is the electric field magnitude equal to one-half the magnitude of the field at the centre of the disk's surface?
items.explain:
On the axis: $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}\right)$; at the surface ($z\to0$) $E_0=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.
$1-\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}=\dfrac12\Rightarrow\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}=\dfrac12\Rightarrow3z^2=R^2$, $z=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}=0.346\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q6

items.q: In Millikan's experiment an oil drop of radius $1.64\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ and density $0.851\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ is held suspended in a DOWNWARD electric field of $1.92\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N/C}$. What is the magnitude of the charge on the drop in units of $e$?
items.explain:
Mass $m=\rho\,\tfrac43\pi r^3=851\times\tfrac43\pi(1.64\times10^{-6})^3=1.57\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
Equilibrium: $|q|E=mg\Rightarrow|q|=\dfrac{(1.57\times10^{-14})(9.8)}{1.92\times10^5}=8.0\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}=5.0\,e$.
The force on the drop must point UP, opposite to the field, so the charge is negative: $q=-5e$.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q7

items.q: An electron between two charged parallel plates is in a uniform field $\vec E=(120\,\mathrm{N/C})\hat j$. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
items.explain: $a=\dfrac{eE}{m}=\dfrac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(120)}{9.11\times10^{-31}}=2.11\times10^{13}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, directed along $-\hat j$ (the force on an electron is opposite to $\vec E$).
items.src: Homework session 2, Q8(a)

items.q: The electron has $v_x=1.5\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $v_y=3.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and accelerates at $-2.11\times10^{13}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ along $y$. What is $v_y$ after its $x$ coordinate has changed by $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$?
items.explain:
The $x$-motion is uniform: $t=\dfrac{0.020}{1.5\times10^5}=1.33\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s}$.
$v_y=3.0\times10^3+(-2.11\times10^{13})(1.33\times10^{-7})=-2.81\times10^6\,\mathrm{m/s}$; $v_x$ is unchanged, so $\vec v=(1.5\times10^5\hat i-2.8\times10^6\hat j)\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q8(b)

items.q: How much work is required to turn an electric dipole through $180^\circ$ in a uniform field of $46.0\,\mathrm{N/C}$ if the dipole moment is $3.02\times10^{-25}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$ and the initial angle between $\vec p$ and $\vec E$ is $64^\circ$?
items.explain:
$U=-pE\cos\theta$. Initially $\theta=64^\circ$, finally $244^\circ$: $W=\Delta U=-pE(\cos244^\circ-\cos64^\circ)=2pE\cos64^\circ$.
$W=2(3.02\times10^{-25})(46.0)\cos64^\circ=1.22\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J}$ (positive work is needed: the dipole prefers $\theta<90^\circ$).
items.src: Homework session 2, Q9

items.q: An electric dipole has moment $p=4.0\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$. What is the magnitude of its field on the perpendicular bisector at a distance $r=0.30\,\mathrm{m}\gg d$ from its centre?
items.explain: Far on the bisector $E=\dfrac{kp}{r^3}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-12})}{0.30^3}=1.33\,\mathrm{N/C}$, pointing OPPOSITE to $\vec p$. (On the axis it is twice as large, $2kp/r^3$.)
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q3

items.q: A dipole consists of $+1.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ and $-1.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ separated by $1.0\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is the magnitude of the field on its axis at $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ from the centre?
items.explain:
Far on the axis $E=\dfrac{2kp}{z^3}$ with $p=qd=1.0\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$: $E=\dfrac{2(8.99\times10^9)(1.0\times10^{-11})}{0.50^3}=1.44\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
Adding the exact fields of the two charges gives the same value to within $0.1\%$. A single charge would give $36\,\mathrm{N/C}$: the two nearly cancel.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q3

items.q: Charges 4 nC (at x = 0) and 4 nC (at x = 0.2 m) lie on the x axis. What is the electric field at the midpoint (positive = towards +x)?
items.explain:
Both distances are 0.1 m. Left charge: $E_a=\dfrac{kq_a}{r^2}=3600\,\mathrm{N/C}$ along $+x$ if $q_a>0$.
Right charge: $E_b=\dfrac{kq_b}{r^2}=3600\,\mathrm{N/C}$, directed along $-x$ if $q_b>0$ (away from a positive charge).
Net $E_x=E_a-E_b=0\,\mathrm{N/C}$: like charges partly cancel at the midpoint, opposite charges add.

items.q: An electron enters the region between horizontal plates at 2\times10^{6} m/s, parallel to them. The uniform field is 500 N/C and the plates are 0.05 m long. By how much is the electron deflected (in mm) when it leaves?

items.q: A water molecule has dipole moment $6.2\times10^{-30}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$. What torque acts on it when it makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with a uniform field of $3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{N/C}$?
items.explain: $\tau=pE\sin\theta=(6.2\times10^{-30})(3.0\times10^4)\sin30^\circ=9.3\times10^{-26}\,\mathrm{N\,m}$; it tries to align $\vec p$ with $\vec E$.
items.src: Lecture Electricity C2 (a dipole in an electric field)

items.q: In a uniform electric field the net force on an electric dipole is
opts: zero, but there is a torque unless $\vec p\parallel\vec E$
items.explain: The two charges feel equal and opposite forces $\pm q\vec E$: no net force, but a torque $\vec\tau=\vec p\times\vec E$ (zero only when $\vec p$ and $\vec E$ are parallel or antiparallel).
items.src: Lecture Electricity C2 (a dipole in an electric field)

items.q: A negative test charge is placed in the field of a positive point charge. The force on the test charge points
opts: in the direction of the field
items.explain: The force on a negative charge is opposite to $\vec E$; $\vec E$ points away from the positive charge, so the force points towards it (attraction).
items.src: Lecture Electricity C2 (the electric field)

items.q: A very long straight wire carries a uniform linear charge density of $5.0\,\mathrm{nC/m}$. What is the field magnitude $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ from the wire?
items.explain: Infinite line: $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}=\dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}=\dfrac{2(8.99\times10^9)(5.0\times10^{-9})}{0.20}=450\,\mathrm{N/C}$, falling off as $1/r$ (not $1/r^2$). (A finite rod gives this limit when $r\ll L$.)
items.src: Lecture Electricity C2 (a line of charge)

items.q: A ring of radius $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a uniformly distributed charge of $3.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. What is the electric field on the axis, $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the centre?
items.explain:
$E=\dfrac{kQz}{(z^2+R^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(3.0\times10^{-9})(0.10)}{(0.010+0.0025)^{3/2}}=1.9\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{N/C}$, along the axis away from the ring.
Treating the ring as a point charge at the centre would give $2.7\times10^3\,\mathrm{N/C}$ - not accurate at $z=2R$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q4

items.q: Charges $+4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ and $+1.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ are $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$ apart. At what distance from the $+4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ charge, between them, is the electric field zero?
items.explain: The fields oppose between like charges; zero when $\dfrac{4}{x^2}=\dfrac{1}{(0.30-x)^2}\Rightarrow0.30-x=\dfrac x2\Rightarrow x=0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ (closer to the smaller charge).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q2

items.q: Charges $+3.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ sit at the two TOP corners and $-3.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ at the two BOTTOM corners of a square of side $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the field magnitude at the centre of the square?
items.explain:
Each corner is at $\dfrac{a}{\sqrt2}$ from the centre: each field has magnitude $\dfrac{kq}{a^2/2}=\dfrac{2kq}{a^2}=1.35\times10^3\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
The horizontal components cancel in pairs; the four vertical components (down, from each charge) add: $E=4\cdot\dfrac{2kq}{a^2}\cos45^\circ=\dfrac{4\sqrt2\,kq}{a^2}=3.8\times10^3\,\mathrm{N/C}$ pointing from the positive towards the negative charges.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q2

items.q: A $2.0\,\mathrm{g}$ charged ball hangs from a light thread in a uniform horizontal field of $1.5\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{N/C}$ and rests with the thread at $20^\circ$ to the vertical. What is its charge?
items.explain: Equilibrium: $T\cos\theta=mg$ and $T\sin\theta=qE$, so $q=\dfrac{mg\tan\theta}{E}=\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{-3})(9.8)\tan20^\circ}{1.5\times10^3}=4.8\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 2, Q7

items.q: A thin rod of length $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a uniformly distributed charge of $4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. What is the field magnitude on the line of the rod, at a point $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ beyond one end?
items.explain:
Integrate $\mathrm{d}E=\dfrac{k\lambda\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^2}$ from $x=d$ to $d+L$: $E=k\lambda\left(\dfrac1d-\dfrac1{d+L}\right)=\dfrac{kQ}{d(d+L)}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-9})}{(0.10)(0.30)}=1.2\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
Using a point charge at the centre ($k Q/(d+L/2)^2=2.2\times10^3\,\mathrm{N/C}$) is not valid so close to the rod.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 1, Chapter 2 Q4

items.q: Which equation gives the force on a charge $q$ placed in an electric field $\vec E$?
opts: $\vec F=q\vec E$ (along $\vec E$ for $q>0$, opposite for $q<0$)
items.explain: The field is defined as force per unit positive test charge, $\vec E=\vec F/q_0$.

items.q: How many times larger is the acceleration of an electron than that of a proton in the same electric field?
items.explain: Same force magnitude $eE$; $a=\dfrac{eE}{m}$, so $\dfrac{a_e}{a_p}=\dfrac{m_p}{m_e}=\dfrac{1.673\times10^{-27}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}=1.84\times10^{3}$ (in opposite directions).

items.q: A proton starts from rest at one plate of a parallel-plate capacitor with uniform field $2.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{N/C}$. How long does it take to cross a gap of $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$?
items.explain:
$a=\dfrac{eE}{m_p}=1.9\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
$d=\tfrac12at^2\Rightarrow t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2d}{a}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.050)}{1.9\times10^{11}}}=7.2\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: A dipole of moment $5.0\times10^{-30}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$ makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with a uniform field of $4.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{N/C}$. What is its potential energy ($U=-\vec p\cdot\vec E$)?
items.explain: $U=-pE\cos\theta=-(5.0\times10^{-30})(4.0\times10^4)\cos60^\circ=-1.0\times10^{-25}\,\mathrm{J}$. Negative: the dipole is below its maximum energy ($+pE$ at $180^\circ$), minimum $-pE$ at $0^\circ$.

items.q: At the centre of a uniformly charged ring the electric field is
opts: zero (the contributions of opposite elements cancel)
items.explain: For every element there is an opposite one producing an equal and opposite field at the centre.

items.q: A positive point charge is released from rest in a non-uniform electric field. It
opts: moves along the field line only if the line is straight
moves perpendicular to the field line
always moves along the field line it started on
items.explain: The initial acceleration is along $\vec E$, but later the velocity is no longer along the (curved) line: the path follows a field line only when the line is straight.

items.q: An electron moving horizontally at $3.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ enters a region of vertical field $2.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{N/C}$ that is $4.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ long. At what angle to its original direction does it leave?
items.explain:
Time in the field $t=\dfrac{L}{v_0}=1.33\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}$; $a=\dfrac{eE}{m}=3.5\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
$v_y=at=4.7\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_y}{v_0}=1.56\Rightarrow\theta=57^\circ$.

items.q: A uniform field of 3000 N/C passes through a flat surface of area 0.2 m². The angle between the field and the surface NORMAL is 60°. What is the flux through the surface?
items.explain:
$\Phi=EA\cos\theta$ with $\theta$ measured from the normal (area vector): $\Phi=3000\times0.2\times\cos60^\circ=300\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$.
If the angle is given from the SURFACE, use the complement.

items.q: A uniform field of 1.2\times10^{4} N/C passes through a flat surface of area 0.04 m². The angle between the field and the surface NORMAL is 45°. What is the flux through the surface?

items.q: A flat surface is parallel to a uniform electric field. The flux through it is
items.explain: The field lines do not cross the surface: the normal is perpendicular to $\vec E$, so $\cos90^\circ=0$ and $\Phi=0$.

items.q: A closed surface encloses a point charge of $+2.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. What is the net electric flux through it?
items.explain: Gauss' law: $\Phi=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-9}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=226\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$, whatever the shape of the surface.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture, 3.2 Gauss' law

items.q: A cube encloses charges of $+5.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ and $-3.0\,\mathrm{nC}$; a $+4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ charge sits outside the cube. What is the net flux through the cube's surface?
items.explain:
Only the ENCLOSED charge counts: $q_{\text{enc}}=5.0-3.0=2.0\,\mathrm{nC}$, so $\Phi=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-9}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=226\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$.
The outside charge makes field lines enter and leave the cube: its net contribution to the flux is zero.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture, 3.2 Gauss' law

items.q: A point charge of $1.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ is at the centre of a cube of side $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the flux through ONE face?
items.explain:
By symmetry the six faces share the total flux equally: $\Phi_{\text{face}}=\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-9}}{6(8.85\times10^{-12})}=18.8\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$.
The side of the cube does not matter. A direct numerical integration of $\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec A$ over one face gives the same value.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture, 3.2 Gauss' law

items.q: Gauss' law $\oint\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec A=q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$ is TRUE for
opts: any closed surface, but it is only USEFUL for finding $E$ when the charge distribution is symmetric
items.explain: It is a general law (one of Maxwell's equations). Symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar) lets us pull $E$ out of the integral and solve for it.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 3.2 Gauss' law

items.q: A very long straight wire has a uniform linear charge density of 2\times10^{-8} C/m. What is the electric field magnitude 0.06 m from the wire?
items.explain:
Cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $\ell$: $E(2\pi r\ell)=\dfrac{\lambda\ell}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}=5990\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
The field falls off as $1/r$. Integrating Coulomb's law along a very long wire gives the same result.

items.q: A very long straight wire has a uniform linear charge density of 5\times10^{-9} C/m. What is the electric field magnitude 0.25 m from the wire?
items.explain:
Cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $\ell$: $E(2\pi r\ell)=\dfrac{\lambda\ell}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}=360\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
The field falls off as $1/r$. Integrating Coulomb's law along a very long wire gives the same result.

items.q: A long thin-walled metal tube of radius $R=3.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ has a charge per unit length $\lambda=2.00\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C/m}$. What is the field magnitude at radial distance $r=2.00R$?
items.explain: Outside the tube a Gaussian cylinder encloses $\lambda\ell$: $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}=\dfrac{2.00\times10^{-8}}{2\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.0600)}=5.99\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{N/C}$.

items.q: For the same metal tube ($R=3.00\,\mathrm{cm}$, $\lambda=2.00\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C/m}$), what is the field magnitude at $r=R/2$ (inside the tube)?
items.explain: A Gaussian cylinder inside the tube encloses no charge (the charge sits on the conductor's surface), so $E=0$.

items.q: Two very long parallel lines of charge are $8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart: line 1 has $+6.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m}$ (at $x=0$) and line 2 has $-2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m}$ (at $x=8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$). At what $x$ along the line joining them is the net field zero?
items.explain:
Between the lines both fields point the same way (away from the positive line, towards the negative one), so they cannot cancel there. Cancellation needs a point beyond the line with the smaller $|\lambda|$.
At $x>8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$: $\dfrac{\lambda_1}{x}=\dfrac{|\lambda_2|}{x-L}$, i.e. $\dfrac{6.0}{x}=\dfrac{2.0}{x-0.080}\Rightarrow x=0.12\,\mathrm{m}=12\,\mathrm{cm}$.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q3

items.q: Two large thin metal plates are parallel and close together; on their inner faces they carry excess surface charge densities of equal magnitude $7.00\times10^{-22}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$ and opposite sign. What is the field magnitude BETWEEN the plates?
items.explain: For a conductor the field next to the surface is $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, and between oppositely charged plates the fields of the two plates add: $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{7.00\times10^{-22}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=7.91\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N/C}$ (zero outside the plates).
items.src: Homework session 2, Q4(c)

items.q: Two large parallel non-conducting sheets carry identical positive uniform surface charge densities $\sigma=1.77\times10^{-22}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$. What is the field magnitude ABOVE both sheets (outside)?
items.explain: Each sheet gives $\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, directed away from it. Outside both sheets the two fields point the same way and add: $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{1.77\times10^{-22}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=2.00\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N/C}$. Between the sheets they cancel.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q5(a)

items.q: Two large parallel sheets carry the SAME uniform positive surface charge density. The field BETWEEN them is
items.explain: Between the sheets the field of each points towards the other sheet, so the two cancel; outside they add to $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q5(b)

items.q: An infinite non-conducting sheet carries a uniform surface charge density of $3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. What is the field magnitude near the sheet?
items.explain: Gaussian 'pillbox': $2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{3.0\times10^{-6}}{2(8.85\times10^{-12})}=1.7\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N/C}$, independent of the distance from the sheet.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 2, Q5

items.q: The surface of a charged conductor carries $2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. What is the field just outside the surface?
items.explain: For a conductor $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-6}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=2.3\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N/C}$, perpendicular to the surface (twice the field of a non-conducting sheet with the same $\sigma$; inside the conductor $E=0$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture, 3.3 A charged isolated conductor

items.q: A solid sphere of radius $a=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a net charge $q_1=5.00\,\mathrm{fC}$ uniformly distributed through its volume. It is concentric with a conducting spherical shell (inner radius $2a$, outer radius $2.4a$, net charge $-q_1$). What is the field magnitude at $r=a/2$?
items.explain:
Gaussian sphere of radius $r$: $E\,4\pi r^2=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}$.
Inside the uniform sphere $q_{\text{enc}}=q_1\dfrac{r^3}{a^3}$, so $E=\dfrac{kq_1r}{a^3}=0.0562\,\mathrm{N/C}$ (grows linearly with $r$).
A numerical integration of Coulomb's law over the volume gives the same field.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q6

items.q: A solid sphere of radius $a=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a net charge $q_1=5.00\,\mathrm{fC}$ uniformly distributed through its volume. It is concentric with a conducting spherical shell (inner radius $2a$, outer radius $2.4a$, net charge $-q_1$). What is the field magnitude at $r=a$?
items.explain:
Gaussian sphere of radius $r$: $E\,4\pi r^2=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}$.
Outside (or at the surface) the whole charge counts: $E=\dfrac{kq_1}{r^2}=0.112\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
A numerical integration of Coulomb's law over the volume gives the same field.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q6

items.q: A solid sphere of radius $a=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a net charge $q_1=5.00\,\mathrm{fC}$ uniformly distributed through its volume. It is concentric with a conducting spherical shell (inner radius $2a$, outer radius $2.4a$, net charge $-q_1$). What is the field magnitude at $r=1.5a$?
items.explain:
Gaussian sphere of radius $r$: $E\,4\pi r^2=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}$.
Outside (or at the surface) the whole charge counts: $E=\dfrac{kq_1}{r^2}=0.0499\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
A numerical integration of Coulomb's law over the volume gives the same field.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q6

items.q: In the same arrangement (solid sphere $q_1=5.00\,\mathrm{fC}$, radius $a=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}$; shell between $2a$ and $2.4a$ with net charge $-q_1$), what is the field magnitude at $r=3.5a$, outside everything?
items.explain: Net enclosed charge $=q_1+(-q_1)=0$, so $E=0$ outside the whole system.
items.src: Homework session 2, Q6(f)

items.q: In the same arrangement (solid sphere with $+5.00\,\mathrm{fC}$ inside a conducting shell of net charge $-5.00\,\mathrm{fC}$), what is the charge on the INNER surface of the shell, in fC?
items.explain: The field inside the conducting material of the shell must be zero. A Gaussian sphere inside the shell must enclose zero charge, so the inner surface carries $-q_1=-5.00\,\mathrm{fC}$. The outer surface then carries $-5.00-(-5.00)=0$.

items.q: A solid NON-conducting sphere of radius 0.1 m carries a uniform volume charge of total 5 nC. What is the field at 0.04 m from the centre (inside)?
items.explain: A Gaussian sphere of radius $r<R$ encloses $q_{\text{enc}}=Q\dfrac{r^3}{R^3}$, so $E=\dfrac{kQr}{R^3}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(5\times10^{-9})(0.04)}{0.1^3}=1800\,\mathrm{N/C}$.

items.q: A solid NON-conducting sphere of radius 0.2 m carries a uniform volume charge of total 8 nC. What is the field at 0.15 m from the centre (inside)?
items.explain: A Gaussian sphere of radius $r<R$ encloses $q_{\text{enc}}=Q\dfrac{r^3}{R^3}$, so $E=\dfrac{kQr}{R^3}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(8\times10^{-9})(0.15)}{0.2^3}=1350\,\mathrm{N/C}$.

items.q: Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is
opts: zero everywhere in the material, and any excess charge sits on the surface
items.explain: If $\vec E$ were non-zero the free charges would move; at equilibrium $\vec E=0$ inside, so by Gauss' law there is no net charge in the interior.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 3.3 A charged isolated conductor

items.q: A point charge $+q$ is placed at the centre of a neutral conducting spherical shell. The charges on the inner and outer surfaces of the shell are
opts: $+q$ on the inner surface and $-q$ on the outer surface
$-q$ on the inner surface and $+q$ on the outer surface
items.explain: A Gaussian sphere inside the metal must enclose zero net charge, so the inner surface carries $-q$; the shell is neutral overall, so $+q$ appears on the outer surface (and the field outside is $kq/r^2$ as if the shell were absent).
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 3.3 A charged isolated conductor

items.q: The flux through a closed spherical surface centred on a point charge $q$ changes when
opts: the radius of the sphere is doubled
the sphere is replaced by a cube enclosing the same charge
the charge is moved off-centre but stays inside
items.explain: $\Phi=q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$ depends only on the enclosed charge: neither the radius, the shape nor the position inside matters.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 3.2 Gauss' law

items.q: A uniform field of $500\,\mathrm{N/C}$ is perpendicular to the flat circular base of a hemisphere of radius $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the magnitude of the flux through the curved surface?
items.explain:
The hemisphere plus its flat base form a closed surface with no enclosed charge, so the total flux is zero: the flux through the curved part equals (in magnitude) that through the base, $E\pi R^2=500\pi(0.10)^2=15.7\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$.
Counting the curved area $2\pi R^2$ would ignore that the field lines are not perpendicular to it.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.1

items.q: A closed cylinder with no charge inside is placed in a uniform electric field. The net flux through its surface is
items.explain: Field lines entering through one part of the surface leave through another. With $q_{\text{enc}}=0$, Gauss' law gives $\Phi=0$.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.2

items.q: A long coaxial cable has an inner conductor with $+3.0\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ and an outer thin shell with $-3.0\,\mathrm{nC/m}$. What is the field magnitude between them at a radius of $5.0\,\mathrm{mm}$?
items.explain: Gaussian cylinder of radius $r$ between the conductors encloses $\lambda\ell$: $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}=\dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}=\dfrac{2(8.99\times10^9)(3.0\times10^{-9})}{0.0050}=1.1\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{N/C}$ (radial). Outside the cable the enclosed charge is zero, so $E=0$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 2, Q2

items.q: A long non-conducting cylinder of radius $3.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a uniform volume charge density $2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^3}$. What is the field magnitude $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the axis (inside)?
items.explain: Gaussian cylinder of radius $r<R$ and length $\ell$ encloses $\rho\pi r^2\ell$: $E\,2\pi r\ell=\dfrac{\rho\pi r^2\ell}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{\rho r}{2\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{-6})(0.020)}{2(8.85\times10^{-12})}=2.3\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{N/C}$ (grows linearly with $r$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.4

items.q: A conducting spherical shell of radius $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a charge of $-6.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. What is the magnitude of its surface charge density?
items.explain: The charge sits on the outer surface of area $4\pi R^2$: $|\sigma|=\dfrac{|Q|}{4\pi R^2}=\dfrac{6.0\times10^{-9}}{4\pi(0.20)^2}=1.2\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$ (its sign is that of $Q$: negative).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.3

items.q: The field just outside the surface of a charged conductor is $3.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N/C}$. What is the local surface charge density?
items.explain: $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow\sigma=\varepsilon_0E=(8.85\times10^{-12})(3.0\times10^5)=2.7\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.3

items.q: The field $0.40\,\mathrm{m}$ from the centre of a uniformly charged sphere is $450\,\mathrm{N/C}$, pointing away from it. What is the total charge on the sphere?
items.explain: $E=\dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\Rightarrow Q=\dfrac{Er^2}{k}=\dfrac{450(0.40)^2}{8.99\times10^9}=8.0\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{C}$ (positive, since the field points outward).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 2, Q6

items.q: A point charge $q$ sits at one CORNER of a cube. What is the total flux through the cube's surface?
items.explain:
Eight identical cubes meeting at the charge would enclose it completely, so each receives $\dfrac18$ of the flux: $\Phi=\dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{4.0\times10^{-9}}{8(8.85\times10^{-12})}=56.5\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$.
(Through each of the three faces that do NOT touch the charge: $\dfrac{q}{24\varepsilon_0}$; the three faces at the corner get zero.)
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.2

items.q: The field on a sphere of radius $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ is radially outward with the same magnitude $800\,\mathrm{N/C}$ everywhere. What charge does the sphere enclose?
items.explain:
$\Phi=E\,4\pi r^2=800\times4\pi(0.10)^2=101\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C}$ (outward, so positive charge).
$q_{\text{enc}}=\varepsilon_0\Phi=(8.85\times10^{-12})(101)=8.9\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.2

items.q: Which Gaussian surface exploits the symmetry of a very long uniformly charged straight wire?
opts: a sphere centred on the wire
a cube around a point of the wire
items.explain: The field has cylindrical symmetry: constant magnitude on a coaxial cylinder and perpendicular to its side, parallel to the end caps (no flux through them).
items.src: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.4

items.q: A hollow conductor (a cavity inside, no charge in the cavity) carries a net charge. The field in the cavity is
opts: zero, and all the charge is on the outer surface
items.explain: A Gaussian surface in the metal around the cavity encloses no charge (the field in the metal is zero), so there is no charge on the cavity wall; with no charge in the cavity the field inside is zero (electrostatic shielding).
items.src: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.3

items.q: The flux through a closed surface is negative when
opts: the net charge inside is positive
the net charge inside is negative
items.explain: By Gauss' law $\Phi=q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$: more lines enter than leave when the enclosed charge is negative.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 3, 3.1

items.q: A large, thin, isolated conducting plate of area $0.50\,\mathrm{m^2}$ (per face) carries a total charge of $4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$. What is the field magnitude just outside one face?
items.explain:
The charge spreads equally over the two faces: $\sigma=\dfrac{Q}{2A}=4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
Next to a conductor $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0A}=\dfrac{4.0\times10^{-6}}{2(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.50)}=4.5\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 2, Q4

items.q: In a region the electric field has components $E_y=E_z=0$ and $E_x=(4.00\,\mathrm{N/C})\,x$ ($x$ in metres). Point A is on the $y$ axis at $y=3.00\,\mathrm{m}$ and point B on the $x$ axis at $x=4.00\,\mathrm{m}$. What is $V_B-V_A$?
items.explain:
$V_B-V_A=-\int_A^B\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec l$. Choose the path A to the origin (along $y$, where $E_y=0$, no contribution) and then along $x$ to B.
$V_B-V_A=-\int_0^{4.00}4.00\,x\,\mathrm{d}x=-2.00(4.00)^2=-32.0\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.src: Homework session 3, Q1

items.q: The ammonia molecule has a permanent dipole moment of $1.47\,\mathrm{D}$ ($1\,\mathrm{D}=3.34\times10^{-30}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$). What is the electric potential due to it at a point $52.0\,\mathrm{nm}$ away along the axis of the dipole ($V=0$ at infinity)?
items.explain:
$p=1.47\times3.34\times10^{-30}=4.91\times10^{-30}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$.
Dipole potential on the axis: $V=\dfrac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(4.91\times10^{-30})}{(52.0\times10^{-9})^2}=1.63\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{V}$ (it falls off as $1/r^2$, faster than a point charge's $1/r$).
items.src: Homework session 3, Q3

items.q: A plastic rod carrying a uniformly distributed charge $Q=-25.6\,\mathrm{pC}$ is bent into a circular arc of radius $R=3.71\,\mathrm{cm}$ and central angle $120^\circ$. What is the electric potential at the centre of curvature P (with $V=0$ at infinity)?
items.explain: Potential is a SCALAR and every element $\mathrm{d}q$ is at the same distance $R$ from P: $V=\dfrac{k}{R}\int\mathrm{d}q=\dfrac{kQ}{R}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(-25.6\times10^{-12})}{0.0371}=-6.20\,\mathrm{V}$. The angle of the arc does not matter.
items.src: Homework session 3, Q4

items.q: In the $xy$ plane the electric potential is $V=(2.0\,\mathrm{V/m^2})x^2-(3.0\,\mathrm{V/m^2})y^2$. What is the magnitude of the electric field at the point $(3.0\,\mathrm{m},\,2.0\,\mathrm{m})$?
items.explain:
$\vec E=-\nabla V$: $E_x=-\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x}=-4.0x=-12\,\mathrm{V/m}$, $E_y=-\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y}=+6.0y=+12\,\mathrm{V/m}$.
$\vec E=(-12\,\hat i+12\,\hat j)\,\mathrm{V/m}$, magnitude $\sqrt{12^2+12^2}=17\,\mathrm{V/m}$, directed $135^\circ$ from $+x$.
items.src: Homework session 3, Q5

items.q: Two tiny metal spheres A ($5.00\,\mathrm{g}$) and B ($10.0\,\mathrm{g}$) carry equal positive charges $q=5.00\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ and are tied by a string of length $d=1.00\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the electric potential energy of the system?
items.src: Homework session 3, Q7(a)

items.q: The string between spheres A ($5.00\,\mathrm{g}$) and B ($10.0\,\mathrm{g}$), each carrying $5.00\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ and $1.00\,\mathrm{m}$ apart, is cut. What is the acceleration of sphere A at that instant?
items.explain:
Coulomb force $F=\dfrac{kq^2}{d^2}=0.225\,\mathrm{N}$ on each sphere.
$a_A=\dfrac{F}{m_A}=\dfrac{0.225}{0.00500}=45.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $a_B=22.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
items.src: Homework session 3, Q7(b)

items.q: After a long time the two spheres of the previous problem (A: $5.00\,\mathrm{g}$, B: $10.0\,\mathrm{g}$, each $5.00\,\mu\mathrm{C}$, initially $1.00\,\mathrm{m}$ apart) are far apart. What is the final speed of sphere A?
items.explain:
Momentum conservation (starting at rest): $m_Av_A=m_Bv_B\Rightarrow v_B=\dfrac{v_A}{2}$.
Energy conservation: $U=\tfrac12m_Av_A^2+\tfrac12m_Bv_B^2=\tfrac12(0.005)v_A^2+\tfrac12(0.010)\dfrac{v_A^2}{4}=0.00375\,v_A^2$.
$v_A=\sqrt{\dfrac{0.225}{0.00375}}=7.74\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $v_B=3.87\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
items.src: Homework session 3, Q7(c)

items.q: Two concentric conducting spherical shells have radii $R_1=0.500\,\mathrm{m}$ and $R_2=1.00\,\mathrm{m}$ and carry uniform charges $q_1=2.00\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ (inner) and $q_2=1.00\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ (outer). With $V=0$ at infinity, what is $V$ at $r=4.00\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain: Outside both shells the system acts as a point charge $q_1+q_2$: $V=\dfrac{k(q_1+q_2)}{r}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(3.00\times10^{-6})}{4.00}=6.74\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.src: Homework session 3, Q8(d)

items.q: For the same shells ($R_1=0.500\,\mathrm{m}$ with $2.00\,\mu\mathrm{C}$, $R_2=1.00\,\mathrm{m}$ with $1.00\,\mu\mathrm{C}$), what is the potential at $r=0.700\,\mathrm{m}$, between the shells?
items.explain:
Between the shells the inner shell acts as a point charge, while the outer shell (all of whose charge is at $R_2>r$) contributes the constant $\dfrac{kq_2}{R_2}$.
$V=\dfrac{kq_1}{r}+\dfrac{kq_2}{R_2}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(2.00\times10^{-6})}{0.700}+\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(1.00\times10^{-6})}{1.00}=2.57\times10^{4}+8.99\times10^{3}=3.47\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.src: Homework session 3, Q8(f)

items.q: For the same shells, what is the potential at $r=0.200\,\mathrm{m}$, inside the inner shell?
items.explain: Inside the inner shell $E=0$, so the potential is constant and equal to its value on the inner shell: $V=\dfrac{kq_1}{R_1}+\dfrac{kq_2}{R_2}=3.60\times10^4+8.99\times10^3=4.50\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{V}$ (the same at $r=0$).
items.src: Homework session 3, Q8(h, i)

items.q: What is the electric potential 0.3 m from a point charge of 5 nC (V = 0 at infinity)?
items.explain: $V=\dfrac{kq}{r}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(5\times10^{-9})}{0.3}=150\,\mathrm{V}$ (a scalar: the sign of the charge is kept).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q2

items.q: What is the electric potential 0.1 m from a point charge of -2 nC (V = 0 at infinity)?
items.explain: $V=\dfrac{kq}{r}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(-2\times10^{-9})}{0.1}=-180\,\mathrm{V}$ (a scalar: the sign of the charge is kept).

items.q: What is the electric potential 0.6 m from a point charge of 12 nC (V = 0 at infinity)?

items.q: Point charges of $+3.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ at $(0,0)$, $-5.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ at $(0.20\,\mathrm{m},0)$ and $+4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ at $(0,0.15\,\mathrm{m})$ are fixed. What is the potential at the point $(0.10\,\mathrm{m},\,0.05\,\mathrm{m})$?
items.explain:
Distances: $r_1=\sqrt{0.10^2+0.05^2}=0.112\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_2=\sqrt{0.10^2+0.05^2}=0.112\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_3=\sqrt{0.10^2+0.10^2}=0.141\,\mathrm{m}$.
Potentials add as numbers (signs included): $V=k\left(\dfrac{q_1}{r_1}+\dfrac{q_2}{r_2}+\dfrac{q_3}{r_3}\right)=93.5\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q2

items.q: Two point charges of 2 μC and -3 μC are 0.5 m apart. What is the electric potential energy of the pair (zero at infinite separation)?
items.explain: $U=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(2\times10^{-6})(-3\times10^{-6})}{0.5}=-0.108\,\mathrm{J}$; negative for opposite charges (bound), positive for like charges (work is needed to bring them together).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q7

items.q: Two point charges of 4 μC and 4 μC are 0.2 m apart. What is the electric potential energy of the pair (zero at infinite separation)?
items.explain: $U=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(4\times10^{-6})(4\times10^{-6})}{0.2}=0.719\,\mathrm{J}$; negative for opposite charges (bound), positive for like charges (work is needed to bring them together).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q7

items.q: Three equal charges of $2.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$. How much work was needed to assemble them from far apart?
items.explain: The potential energy is the sum over the THREE pairs: $U=3\,\dfrac{kq^2}{a}=3\,\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-9})^2}{0.10}=1.1\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{J}$ (equal to the work needed to assemble the charges).

items.q: A electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1500 V. What is its final speed (non-relativistic)?
items.explain: Energy conservation: $qV=\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qV}{m}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(1.602\times10^{-19})(1500)}{9.11\times10^{-31}}}=2.3\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: A proton is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 5000 V. What is its final speed (non-relativistic)?
items.explain: Energy conservation: $qV=\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qV}{m}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(1.602\times10^{-19})(5000)}{1.67\times10^{-27}}}=9.79\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: An electron moves through a potential difference of $200\,\mathrm{V}$. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
items.explain: $\Delta K=-q\Delta V=e(200\,\mathrm{V})=3.2\times10^{-17}\,\mathrm{J}$ ($=200\,\mathrm{eV}$).

items.q: A uniform field of $400\,\mathrm{V/m}$ exists between two plates $2.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart. What is the potential difference between the plates?

items.q: A disk of radius $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a uniform surface charge density $1.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. What is the potential on its axis $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ from its centre?
items.explain:
Add the potentials of rings: $V=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{z^2+R^2}-z\right)=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-6}}{2(8.85\times10^{-12})}(0.361-0.200)=9.1\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{V}$.
Numerical integration of the ring contributions gives the same value; treating the disk as a point charge ($k\sigma\pi R^2/z=1.3\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{V}$) is too crude at $z=0.67R$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture, 4.3 Calculations of potential

items.q: A conducting sphere of radius $15\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a charge of $6.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. What is its potential (with $V=0$ at infinity)?
items.explain: The sphere is an equipotential, equal to the value at its surface: $V=\dfrac{kQ}{R}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(6.0\times10^{-9})}{0.15}=3.6\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{V}$ (also the value anywhere inside).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture, 4.6 Potential of a charged isolated conductor

items.q: Two conducting spheres of radii $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $15\,\mathrm{cm}$, far apart, are joined by a long thin wire and given a total charge of $8.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. How much charge ends up on the SMALLER sphere (in nC)?
items.explain:
Joined by a wire the spheres have the same potential: $\dfrac{kq_1}{R_1}=\dfrac{kq_2}{R_2}\Rightarrow q\propto R$.
$q_1=Q\dfrac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}=8.0\times\dfrac{5}{20}=2.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ (and $6.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ on the large one). The smaller sphere has the larger surface charge density, hence the stronger field (points discharge easily).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture, 4.6 Potential of a charged isolated conductor

items.q: Which statement about equipotential surfaces is correct?
opts: Work is needed to move a charge along them
The electric field is perpendicular to them, and no work is done moving a charge along one
The electric field is parallel to them
They cross wherever the field is strong
items.explain: $\Delta V=-\int\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec l=0$ along the surface, so $\vec E$ has no component along it: it is perpendicular. Two equipotentials never cross (V would have two values at one point).
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 4.2 Equipotential surfaces

items.q: At a point where the electric potential is zero, the electric field
opts: must be directed along the potential gradient only if the charge is negative
items.explain: $\vec E=-\nabla V$ depends on how $V$ CHANGES, not on its value. Example: the midpoint of an electric dipole has $V=0$ but $E\neq0$.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 4.4 Calculating the field from the potential

items.q: A positive charge is released from rest in an electric field. It moves towards a region of
opts: lower electric potential (and lower potential energy)
items.explain: The field force on a positive charge points along $\vec E$, i.e. toward decreasing potential; the charge gains kinetic energy and loses potential energy $qV$. A negative charge moves towards higher potential.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 4.1 Potential energy

items.q: The electronvolt (eV) is a unit of
items.explain: An eV is the energy gained by one elementary charge moving through one volt: $e\times1\,\mathrm{V}=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture, 4.1 Potential energy

items.q: A ring of radius $0.06\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a uniformly distributed charge of $5.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. What is the potential on its axis, $0.08\,\mathrm{m}$ from the centre?
items.explain: Every element of the ring is at the same distance $\sqrt{R^2+z^2}=0.10\,\mathrm{m}$, so $V=\dfrac{kQ}{\sqrt{R^2+z^2}}=\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(5.0\times10^{-9})}{0.10}=4.5\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{V}$ (no vector sum needed for a scalar).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 4, 4.3

items.q: A charge of $+2.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ moves from a point at $200\,\mathrm{V}$ to a point at $50\,\mathrm{V}$. How much work does the electric field do on it?
items.explain: $W_{\text{field}}=-\Delta U=-q(V_f-V_i)=q(V_i-V_f)=(2.0\times10^{-6})(150)=3.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ (positive: the charge moves 'downhill' in potential, gaining kinetic energy).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 4, 4.1

items.q: Four charges of $+2.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ sit at the corners of a square of side $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the potential at the centre ($V=0$ at infinity)?
items.explain: Each corner is $\dfrac{a}{\sqrt2}=0.141\,\mathrm{m}$ from the centre. Potentials are scalars and simply add: $V=4\,\dfrac{kq}{a/\sqrt2}=4\,\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-9})}{0.141}=5.1\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{V}$. (The FIELD at the centre is zero, the potential is not.)
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q6

items.q: Charges $+q$ and $-q$ form an electric dipole. The electric potential on the perpendicular bisector of the dipole (at any distance) is
items.explain: Every point of the bisector is equidistant from the two charges, so $V=\dfrac{kq}{r}-\dfrac{kq}{r}=0$ (although the field there is not zero).

items.q: An electron is released from rest and accelerates through $10\,\mathrm{V}$. What is its speed?
items.explain: $eV=\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(1.602\times10^{-19})(10)}{9.11\times10^{-31}}}=1.9\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: Equipotential lines in a uniform field are drawn at $5.0\,\mathrm{V}$ intervals and are $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart. What is the field magnitude?
items.explain: $E=\dfrac{|\Delta V|}{\Delta d}=\dfrac{5.0}{0.020}=250\,\mathrm{V/m}$ (perpendicular to the lines, towards lower potential).
