items.q: Two protons are released from rest $1.0\,\mathrm{nm}$ apart. What is the speed of each when they are very far apart?
items.explain: Energy: $\dfrac{ke^2}{r}=2\times\tfrac12m_pv^2$ (two equal masses, equal speeds), so $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{ke^2}{m_pr}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{(1.673\times10^{-27})(1.0\times10^{-9})}}=1.2\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Using all of $U$ for one proton would give $\sqrt2$ too much.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q7

items.q: A proton is fired from far away at $2.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ straight at a fixed second proton. How close does it get (distance of closest approach)?
items.explain:
At the turning point all the kinetic energy has become electric potential energy: $\tfrac12m_pv_0^2=\dfrac{ke^2}{r_{\min}}$.
$r_{\min}=\dfrac{2ke^2}{m_pv_0^2}=\dfrac{2(8.99\times10^9)(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{(1.673\times10^{-27})(2.0\times10^5)^2}=6.9\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q7

items.q: A uniform field of $300\,\mathrm{V/m}$ points along $+x$. What is $V_B-V_A$ if B is displaced $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ from A at $30^\circ$ to the field direction?
items.explain: $V_B-V_A=-\vec E\cdot\Delta\vec r=-Ed\cos\theta=-(300)(0.20)\cos30^\circ=-52\,\mathrm{V}$ (moving along the field lowers the potential).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q1

items.q: Two parallel plates $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart are held at a potential difference of $300\,\mathrm{V}$. What is the field between them?
items.explain: $E=\dfrac{\Delta V}{d}=\dfrac{300}{0.020}=1.5\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{V/m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q1

items.q: A point charge of $8.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ creates a field. What is the potential difference between a point $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ from it and a point $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ from it ($V_a-V_b$)?
items.explain: $V_a-V_b=kq\left(\dfrac1{r_a}-\dfrac1{r_b}\right)=(8.99\times10^9)(8.0\times10^{-9})\left(\dfrac1{0.20}-\dfrac1{0.50}\right)=2.2\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{V}$ (the point nearer a positive charge is at the higher potential).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Homework session 3, Q2

items.q: If the electric potential is constant throughout a region, the electric field there is
items.explain: $\vec E=-\nabla V=0$ when $V$ does not vary.
items.src: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 4, 4.4

items.q: A charge is moved along an equipotential surface from one point to another. The work done by the electric field is
items.explain: $W=-q\Delta V=0$ since $\Delta V=0$ between any two points of an equipotential surface (the field is perpendicular to the path).
items.src: Electrostatics lecture (2025-26), chapter 4, 4.2

items.q: An electron has velocity $\vec v=(2.0\times10^{6}\hat i+3.0\times10^{6}\hat j)\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a uniform field $\vec B=(0.030\,\hat i-0.15\,\hat j)\,\mathrm{T}$. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it?
items.explain:
$\vec F=q\,\vec v\times\vec B$ with $q=-e$. Both vectors lie in the $xy$ plane, so the cross product points along $z$: $(\vec v\times\vec B)_z=v_xB_y-v_yB_x=(2.0\times10^6)(-0.15)-(3.0\times10^6)(0.030)=-3.9\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{T\,m/s}$.
$|F|=e\,(3.9\times10^5)=6.2\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{N}$.
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 1

items.q: For the electron of the previous problem ($\vec v$ and $\vec B$ both in the $xy$ plane, $(\vec v\times\vec B)_z<0$), the force points along
opts: $-\hat k$ for the electron and $+\hat k$ for a proton
$+\hat k$ for the electron and $-\hat k$ for a proton
items.explain: $\vec v\times\vec B=-3.9\times10^{5}\,\hat k$. For a positive charge $\vec F\parallel\vec v\times\vec B$ (that is $-\hat k$); for the electron the force is reversed: $+\hat k$ (out of the plane).
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 1(b)

items.q: A proton moves at $3.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $30^\circ$ to a uniform $0.40\,\mathrm{T}$ magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on it?
items.explain: $F=qvB\sin\theta=(1.602\times10^{-19})(3.0\times10^6)(0.40)\sin30^\circ=9.6\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{N}$. It is perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec B$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 1

items.q: An electron with kinetic energy $1.0\,\mathrm{keV}$ moves perpendicular to a uniform field of $0.010\,\mathrm{T}$. What is the radius of its circular path?
items.explain:
Speed from the energy: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(1.0\times10^3)(1.602\times10^{-19})}{9.11\times10^{-31}}}=1.9\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: $evB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{mv}{eB}=\dfrac{(9.11\times10^{-31})(1.88\times10^7)}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.010)}=1.1\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}$. A numerical integration of the Lorentz force reproduces this radius.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.2 (charged particle in a magnetic field)

items.q: What is the period of the circular motion of that electron in the $0.010\,\mathrm{T}$ field?
items.explain: $T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}=\dfrac{2\pi m}{eB}=\dfrac{2\pi(9.11\times10^{-31})}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.010)}=3.6\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{s}$ - independent of the speed (so $f=\dfrac{eB}{2\pi m}=2.8\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{Hz}$).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.2 and 5.8 (cyclotron frequency)

items.q: A proton moves in a circle in a uniform field of $1.5\,\mathrm{T}$. What is its cyclotron frequency?
items.explain: $f=\dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}=\dfrac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(1.5)}{2\pi(1.673\times10^{-27})}=2.3\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ ($23\,\mathrm{MHz}$), whatever the proton's speed. ($qB/m$ is the angular frequency, $2\pi f$.)
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.8 (cyclotrons)

items.q: A proton travelling at $2.0\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ enters a uniform field of $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$ at right angles to it. What is the radius of its path?
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.2

items.q: An electron with speed $2.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ enters a uniform field of $1.0\,\mathrm{mT}$ at $30^\circ$ to the field. What is the radius of its helical path?
items.explain:
Only the component of velocity PERPENDICULAR to $\vec B$ makes it circle: $v_\perp=v\sin30^\circ=1.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$r=\dfrac{mv_\perp}{eB}=\dfrac{(9.11\times10^{-31})(1.0\times10^6)}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(1.0\times10^{-3})}=5.7\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.2

items.q: For the same electron (speed $2.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $30^\circ$ to a $1.0\,\mathrm{mT}$ field), what is the pitch of the helix (distance advanced along $\vec B$ per turn)?
items.explain:
The period is $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{eB}=3.6\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}$; along the field the motion is uniform at $v_\parallel=v\cos30^\circ=1.73\times10^6\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$p=v_\parallel T=(1.73\times10^{6})(3.57\times10^{-8})=6.2\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.2

items.q: Charged particles pass undeflected through crossed fields $E=5.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and $B=0.25\,\mathrm{T}$ (velocity selector). What is their speed?
items.explain: No deflection when the electric and magnetic forces cancel: $qE=qvB\Rightarrow v=\dfrac EB=\dfrac{5.0\times10^4}{0.25}=2.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (independent of the charge and the mass).
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Thomson apparatus (crossed fields)

items.q: A singly charged ion of mass $2.0\times10^{-26}\,\mathrm{kg}$ is accelerated from rest through $1000\,\mathrm{V}$ and then enters a uniform field of $0.10\,\mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to its velocity (mass spectrometer). What is the radius of its path?
items.explain:
Energy: $\tfrac12mv^2=eV\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}}=1.26\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$r=\dfrac{mv}{eB}=\dfrac1B\sqrt{\dfrac{2mV}{e}}=\dfrac{1}{0.10}\sqrt{\dfrac{2(2.0\times10^{-26})(1000)}{1.602\times10^{-19}}}=0.16\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, motion of charges in E and B

items.q: An electron has initial velocity $(12.0\,\hat j+15.0\,\hat k)\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and constant acceleration $(2.00\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m/s^2})\hat i$ in a region of uniform fields. If $\vec B=(400\,\mu\mathrm{T})\,\hat i$, what is the electric field $\vec E$?
items.explain:
Newton's second law: $m\vec a=q(\vec E+\vec v\times\vec B)$ with $q=-e$, so $\vec E=-\dfrac me\vec a-\vec v\times\vec B$.
$\vec v\times\vec B=(0,\ 6.00,\ -4.80)\,\mathrm{N/C}$ and $-\dfrac{m}{e}\vec a=-11.4\,\hat i\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
$\vec E=(-11.4\,\hat i-6.00\,\hat j+4.80\,\hat k)\,\mathrm{N/C}$.
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 7

items.q: A horizontal power line carries $5000\,\mathrm{A}$ from south to north. Earth's field ($60.0\,\mu\mathrm{T}$) points north and is inclined $70.0^\circ$ below the horizontal. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on $100\,\mathrm{m}$ of the line?
items.explain:
$F=ILB\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ the angle between the current (north) and the field: $70.0^\circ$.
$F=(5000)(100)(60.0\times10^{-6})\sin70^\circ=28.2\,\mathrm{N}$ (about $0.28\,\mathrm{N}$ per metre).
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 2

items.q: For the same line (current towards the north, Earth's field towards the north and downwards), the direction of the magnetic force is
items.explain: $\vec F=I\vec L\times\vec B$. With north $=\hat y$, east $=\hat x$, up $=\hat z$: $\vec B\propto(\cos70^\circ\hat y-\sin70^\circ\hat z)$ and $\hat y\times(-\hat z)=-\hat x$: the force points west.
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 2(b)

items.q: A 0.5 m straight wire carrying 4 A makes an angle of 90° with a uniform 0.3 T magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on the wire?
items.explain: $F=ILB\sin\theta=4\times0.5\times0.3\times\sin90^\circ=0.6\,\mathrm{N}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 2

items.q: A 0.8 m straight wire carrying 6 A makes an angle of 30° with a uniform 0.25 T magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on the wire?
items.explain: $F=ILB\sin\theta=6\times0.8\times0.25\times\sin30^\circ=0.6\,\mathrm{N}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 2

items.q: A circular loop of radius $8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a current of $0.20\,\mathrm{A}$. Its magnetic moment points along the unit vector $0.60\,\hat i-0.80\,\hat j$. The loop is in a uniform field $\vec B=(0.25\,\hat i+0.30\,\hat k)\,\mathrm{T}$. What is the magnitude of the torque on the loop?
items.explain:
$\mu=IA=I\pi r^2=(0.20)\pi(0.080)^2=4.02\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$, so $\vec\mu=(2.41\times10^{-3}\hat i-3.22\times10^{-3}\hat j)\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$.
$\vec\tau=\vec\mu\times\vec B=(-9.65\times10^{-4}\hat i-7.24\times10^{-4}\hat j+8.04\times10^{-4}\hat k)\,\mathrm{N\,m}$, magnitude $1.45\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N\,m}$.
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 3

items.q: For the same loop and field ($\vec\mu=(2.41\times10^{-3}\hat i-3.22\times10^{-3}\hat j)\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$, $\vec B=(0.25\hat i+0.30\hat k)\,\mathrm{T}$), what is the orientation energy $U=-\vec\mu\cdot\vec B$?
items.explain: $\vec\mu\cdot\vec B=(2.41\times10^{-3})(0.25)+0+0=6.03\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J/T\cdot T}$, so $U=-6.03\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$.
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 3(b)

items.q: A rectangular coil of $100$ turns, $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}\times8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$, carries $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in a uniform field of $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$ that lies IN the plane of the coil. What is the torque on it?
items.explain: $\mu=NIA=100(2.0)(0.050)(0.080)=0.80\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$. Field in the plane of the coil means $\vec B\perp\vec\mu$: $\tau=\mu B\sin90^\circ=(0.80)(0.50)=0.40\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ (the maximum torque; zero when the coil faces the field).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 3

items.q: A copper strip ($n=8.5\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$) $0.10\,\mathrm{mm}$ thick carries $10\,\mathrm{A}$ in a field of $1.0\,\mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to its faces. What is the Hall voltage across the strip?
items.explain: $V_H=\dfrac{IB}{ne\,t}=\dfrac{(10)(1.0)}{(8.5\times10^{28})(1.602\times10^{-19})(1.0\times10^{-4})}=7.3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{V}$ - only a few microvolts in a good conductor, because $n$ is so large (semiconductors have far larger Hall voltages).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.7 (the Hall effect)

items.q: A cyclotron with a magnetic field of $1.2\,\mathrm{T}$ and a radius of $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ accelerates protons. What is their maximum kinetic energy, in MeV?
items.explain:
At the largest radius $r=R=\dfrac{mv}{eB}\Rightarrow v=\dfrac{eBR}{m}$.
$K=\dfrac{(eBR)^2}{2m}=\dfrac{[(1.602\times10^{-19})(1.2)(0.50)]^2}{2(1.673\times10^{-27})}=2.8\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{J}=17\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.8 (cyclotrons)

items.q: A magnetic field does NO work on a charged particle because
opts: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity
items.explain: $\mathrm{d}W=\vec F\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec l=q(\vec v\times\vec B)\cdot\vec v\,\mathrm{d}t=0$: the force changes the direction of the velocity, never its magnitude, so the kinetic energy is constant.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.2

items.q: A charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is
items.explain: $F=qvB\sin\theta$ and $\theta=0$: no force, so the particle keeps moving in a straight line.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.1

items.q: Two particles of the same charge and speed enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it; particle 2 has twice the mass of particle 1. The ratio of the radii $r_2/r_1$ is
items.explain: $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}\propto m$ at fixed $q$, $v$, $B$, so $\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}=\dfrac{2m}{m}=2$.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.2

items.q: In a velocity selector with crossed $\vec E$ and $\vec B$, particles of which speed pass straight through?
opts: all speeds, if the charge is large enough
items.explain: The two forces $qE$ and $qvB$ are opposite and balance only when $v=E/B$.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.6 (discovery of the electron)

items.q: Two long parallel wires $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart carry $20\,\mathrm{A}$ and $30\,\mathrm{A}$ in the same direction. What is the magnitude of the force per unit length on each wire?
items.explain:
The field of wire 1 at wire 2 is $B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi d}$; the force per length on wire 2 is $I_2B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(20)(30)}{2\pi(0.050)}=2.4\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N/m}$.
Parallel currents ATTRACT (antiparallel currents repel); the two forces are equal and opposite.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.5 (force between parallel currents)

items.q: Three long parallel wires in a plane, $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ apart (a, b, c in a row), all carry $8.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in the same direction. What is the net force per metre on the OUTER wire a?
items.explain:
Wire b (distance $d$) attracts a with $\dfrac{\mu_0I^2}{2\pi d}=1.28\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{N/m}$; wire c (distance $2d$) attracts it with half that. Both pull towards the other wires, so they add: $\dfrac32\cdot\dfrac{\mu_0I^2}{2\pi d}=1.9\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{N/m}$.
(The force on the middle wire is zero by symmetry.)
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, parallel wires (net force on wire a)

items.q: A proton moves along the +x axis in a uniform magnetic field along the +y axis. In which direction is the magnetic force on it?
items.explain:
$\vec F=q\,\vec v\times\vec B$. For the unit vectors, $\vec v\times\vec B$ points along +z.
The charge is positive: the same direction, so the force points along +z.

items.q: A proton and an alpha particle (charge $2e$, mass $4m_p$) have the SAME kinetic energy and enter a uniform field perpendicular to it. The ratio $r_\alpha/r_p$ is
items.explain: $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$. With equal $K$: $\dfrac{r_\alpha}{r_p}=\dfrac{\sqrt{m_\alpha}}{\sqrt{m_p}}\dfrac{q_p}{q_\alpha}=\sqrt4\cdot\dfrac12=1$: the two follow the same circle.

items.q: How long does a proton take to complete HALF a circle in a uniform $0.80\,\mathrm{T}$ field?
items.explain: The period is $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{eB}$, so half a circle takes $\dfrac T2=\dfrac{\pi m}{eB}=\dfrac{\pi(1.673\times10^{-27})}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.80)}=4.1\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}$, whatever the speed.

items.q: Singly charged ions of $^{235}$U and $^{238}$U enter the same magnetic field perpendicular to it with the same kinetic energy. The $^{235}$U ions follow a semicircle of radius $1.00\,\mathrm{m}$. How far apart do the two beams land on the detector (the difference of the diameters)?
items.explain:
$r=\dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}\propto\sqrt m$: $r_{238}=1.00\sqrt{\dfrac{238}{235}}=1.0063\,\mathrm{m}$.
The landing points are one DIAMETER from the entrance: $2(1.0063-1.00)=0.0127\,\mathrm{m}=1.3\,\mathrm{cm}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.6 (mass-to-charge ratio)

items.q: A wire carrying $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$ is bent into a semicircle of radius $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ lying in a plane perpendicular to a uniform $0.40\,\mathrm{T}$ field. What is the net magnetic force on the semicircle?
items.explain: The net force on a curved wire equals the force on a straight wire joining its ends: $F=I\,(2R)\,B=(3.0)(0.20)(0.40)=0.24\,\mathrm{N}$. The arc length $\pi R$ is NOT the effective length.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 2

items.q: The net magnetic force on a closed current loop in a UNIFORM magnetic field is
opts: perpendicular to the plane of the loop
zero (but there may be a torque)
items.explain: The forces on opposite sides are equal and opposite, so the net force vanishes: $\oint I\,\mathrm{d}\vec l\times\vec B=I\left(\oint\mathrm{d}\vec l\right)\times\vec B=0$. The forces can still form a couple (torque $\vec\mu\times\vec B$).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.4 (torque on a current loop)

items.q: A coil with magnetic moment $0.80\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$ makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with a $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$ field. What is the magnitude of the torque?
items.explain: $\tau=\mu B\sin\theta=(0.80)(0.50)\sin30^\circ=0.20\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ (with $\theta$ the angle between $\vec\mu$ and $\vec B$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.4

items.q: A coil with magnetic moment $0.80\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$ is in a $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$ field. How much work is needed to turn it from parallel to $\vec B$ (stable) to antiparallel (unstable)?
items.explain: $U=-\vec\mu\cdot\vec B$: $U_{\parallel}=-\mu B$ and $U_{\text{anti}}=+\mu B$, so $W=\Delta U=2\mu B=2(0.80)(0.50)=0.80\,\mathrm{J}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.4

items.q: In the Bohr model the electron circles the proton at $2.19\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in an orbit of radius $5.29\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the orbital magnetic dipole moment?
items.explain: Orbiting charge is a current $I=\dfrac{e}{T}=\dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$; $\mu=IA=\dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\pi r^2=\dfrac{evr}{2}=\dfrac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(2.19\times10^6)(5.29\times10^{-11})}{2}=9.3\times10^{-24}\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$ (the Bohr magneton).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.4

items.q: A metal strip $0.20\,\mathrm{mm}$ thick carries $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in a perpendicular field of $1.5\,\mathrm{T}$ and shows a Hall voltage of $20\,\mu\mathrm{V}$. What is the density of charge carriers?
items.explain: $V_H=\dfrac{IB}{net}\Rightarrow n=\dfrac{IB}{etV_H}=\dfrac{(3.0)(1.5)}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(2.0\times10^{-4})(2.0\times10^{-5})}=7.0\times10^{27}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$.

items.q: The sign of the Hall voltage across a conducting strip tells us
opts: the strength of the current only
the direction of the electric field in the strip
whether the charge carriers are positive or negative
items.explain: Moving positive or negative carriers are pushed to the same side by the magnetic force but produce opposite polarity of the transverse voltage: the Hall effect identified electrons as the carriers in most metals.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.7

items.q: Electrons accelerated from rest through $2000\,\mathrm{V}$ move in a circle of radius $0.151\,\mathrm{m}$ in a field of $1.0\,\mathrm{mT}$. What value of $e/m$ follows from these three numbers?
items.explain: $eV=\tfrac12mv^2$ and $r=\dfrac{mv}{eB}$: eliminate $v$ to get $\dfrac em=\dfrac{2V}{B^2r^2}=\dfrac{2(2000)}{(1.0\times10^{-3})^2(0.151)^2}=1.75\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{C/kg}$ (accepted value $1.76\times10^{11}$) - Thomson's method.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.6 (discovery of the electron)

items.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in OPPOSITE directions. The force between them is
items.explain: Parallel currents attract, antiparallel currents repel.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.5

items.q: Two long parallel wires $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ apart each carry $1.0\,\mathrm{A}$. What is the force per metre between them? (This defined the ampere.)
items.explain: $\dfrac FL=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1)(1)}{2\pi(1)}=2\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{N/m}$.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 5, 5.5

items.topic: Magnetic field of a straight wire
items.q: What is the magnetic field $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ from a long straight wire carrying $5.0\,\mathrm{A}$?
items.explain: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(5.0)}{2\pi(0.10)}=1.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$; the field lines are circles around the wire (right-hand rule).

items.q: A coil has $100$ circular turns of radius $0.60\,\mathrm{m}$, each carrying $5.0\,\mathrm{A}$. What is the magnetic field at its centre?
items.explain: One loop gives $B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}$ at the centre; $N$ turns multiply it: $B=\dfrac{N\mu_0I}{2R}=\dfrac{100(4\pi\times10^{-7})(5.0)}{2(0.60)}=5.2\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}$. A numerical Biot-Savart summation around the loop gives the same value.
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Example 6.2.2

items.q: For the same coil ($100$ turns, $R=0.60\,\mathrm{m}$, $5.0\,\mathrm{A}$), what is the field on the axis $0.80\,\mathrm{m}$ from the centre?
items.explain:
On the axis: $B=\dfrac{N\mu_0IR^2}{2(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{100(4\pi\times10^{-7})(5.0)(0.36)}{2(0.36+0.64)^{3/2}}=1.1\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}$.
Check by summing Biot-Savart contributions numerically: same value. At $z\gg R$ this tends to the dipole form $\dfrac{N\mu_0IR^2}{2z^3}$.
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Example 6.2.2(b)

items.q: A wire carrying $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$ is bent into a quarter circle of radius $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ (the straight leads point towards the centre and contribute nothing). What is the field at the centre of the arc?
items.explain: An arc of angle $\varphi$ gives the fraction $\dfrac{\varphi}{2\pi}$ of a full loop: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0I\varphi}{4\pi R}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.0)(\pi/2)}{4\pi(0.20)}=2.4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}$ (verified by direct numerical summation).
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, magnetic field from an arc of current

items.q: A straight wire segment of length $0.40\,\mathrm{m}$ carries $6.0\,\mathrm{A}$. What is the field at a point $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from it on its perpendicular bisector?
items.explain:
Biot-Savart for a finite segment: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi a}(\sin\theta_1+\sin\theta_2)$ with $\sin\theta=\dfrac{L/2}{\sqrt{a^2+(L/2)^2}}=0.97$ at each end.
$B=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(6.0)}{4\pi(0.050)}(2)(0.970)=2.3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$, only 3% below the infinite-wire value $2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Biot-Savart law

items.topic: Magnetic field of a straight wire
items.q: Two long parallel wires $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ apart carry $10\,\mathrm{A}$ in OPPOSITE directions. What is the magnetic field midway between them?
items.explain: Each wire gives $\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi(d/2)}=2.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ at the midpoint. For opposite currents the two fields point the SAME way between the wires and add: $4.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ (for parallel currents they would cancel to zero).

items.topic: Magnetic field of a straight wire
items.q: Two long parallel wires carry equal currents in the SAME direction. The magnetic field midway between them is
opts: equal to that of one wire
items.explain: At the midpoint the fields of the two wires have equal magnitude and opposite directions.

items.topic: Magnetic field of a straight wire

opts: straight lines parallel to the wire
straight lines radiating from the wire
closed lines only inside the wire

items.explain: Thumb along the current, fingers curl in the direction of $\vec B$.

items.q: Gauss' law for magnetism, $\oint\vec B\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec A=0$, states that
opts: there are no magnetic monopoles: field lines are closed loops
the magnetic flux through a closed surface equals $\mu_0I$
items.explain: Every field line that enters a closed surface also leaves it, because magnetic poles come in N-S pairs.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 6, 6.2

items.q: Eight long wires cross the page perpendicularly; wire $k$ ($k=1,\dots,8$) carries a current $k\,i$ with $i=4.50\,\mathrm{mA}$: out of the page for odd $k$ and into the page for even $k$. A counter-clockwise closed path encloses wires $1,3,4$ and $6$ only. What is $\oint\vec B\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s$ along it?
items.explain:
Right-hand rule: for a counter-clockwise path, currents OUT of the page count positive and currents into the page negative.
$I_{\text{enc}}=(1+3-4-6)\,i=-6i=-27.0\,\mathrm{mA}$.
$\oint\vec B\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s=\mu_0I_{\text{enc}}=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(-0.0270)=-3.4\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{T\,m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Question 6 (eight wires)

items.q: A closed loop encloses three long wires carrying $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$ (both out of the page) and $1.5\,\mathrm{A}$ (into the page), and a fourth wire of $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$ lies outside the loop. What is $\oint\vec B\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s$ (counter-clockwise)?
items.explain:
Only enclosed currents count, with signs: $I_{\text{enc}}=2.0+3.0-1.5=3.5\,\mathrm{A}$ (the outside wire contributes to $\vec B$ on the path but not to the integral).
$\oint\vec B\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s=\mu_0(3.5)=4.4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T\,m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism tutoring slides, Ampere's law

items.q: A $15.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ long solenoid of radius $0.750\,\mathrm{cm}$ is closely wound with $600$ turns and carries $8.00\,\mathrm{A}$. What is the magnetic field near its centre?
items.explain: $B=\mu_0nI$ with $n=\dfrac NL=\dfrac{600}{0.150}=4000\,\mathrm{turns/m}$: $B=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(4000)(8.00)=4.02\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}$ (the radius does not matter for a long solenoid).
items.src: Magnetism tutoring slides, Young and Freedman 28.42

items.q: A toroid with $500$ turns carrying $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ has its field measured at radius $15\,\mathrm{cm}$ inside the core. What is the field?
items.explain: Ampère's law on a circle of radius $r$: $B(2\pi r)=\mu_0NI\Rightarrow B=\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2\pi r}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(500)(2.0)}{2\pi(0.15)}=1.3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}$ (falls as $1/r$ across the core; zero outside it).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 6, 6.3 solenoids and toroid

items.q: A long straight wire of radius $2.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ carries $8.0\,\mathrm{A}$ uniformly over its cross-section. What is the magnetic field at a distance of 1 mm from the axis?
items.explain: Inside the wire the enclosed current is $I\dfrac{r^2}{R^2}$: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0Ir}{2\pi R^2}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(8.0)(1.0\times10^{-3})}{2\pi(2.0\times10^{-3})^2}=4.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}$ (it grows linearly with $r$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 6, 6.2 Ampere's law

items.q: A long straight wire of radius $2.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ carries $8.0\,\mathrm{A}$ uniformly over its cross-section. What is the magnetic field at a distance of 4 mm from the axis?
items.explain: Outside the wire the whole current is enclosed: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(8.0)}{2\pi(4.0\times10^{-3})}=4.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}$ (falls as $1/r$). The two formulas agree at the surface.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 6, 6.2 Ampere's law

items.q: The magnetic field inside a long ideal solenoid is
opts: proportional to the distance from the axis
uniform, parallel to the axis, and zero outside
items.explain: $B=\mu_0nI$ along the axis everywhere inside; the outside field of an ideal long solenoid is negligible.

items.q: To find the magnetic field of a long solenoid with Ampère's law, the best amperian loop is
opts: a circle around the solenoid's axis
a rectangle with one long side inside the solenoid, parallel to its axis
items.explain: Along the long inside side $B$ is uniform and parallel to the path; the short sides are perpendicular to $\vec B$ (no contribution) and the outside side has $B\approx0$: $BL=\mu_0nLI$.

items.q: The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field of a current element $I\,\mathrm{d}\vec s$ as
items.explain: It is the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law, but with a CROSS product: $\mathrm{d}\vec B$ is perpendicular to both the current element and $\hat r$.

items.topic: Magnetic field of a straight wire
items.q: A long straight wire along the z axis carries current in the +z direction. In which direction is its magnetic field at a point on the +x axis?
items.explain:
Biot-Savart: $\mathrm{d}\vec B\propto\mathrm{d}\vec s\times\hat r$ with $\mathrm{d}\vec s$ along +z and $\hat r$ (from the wire to the point) along +x.
The cross product points along +y (right-hand rule: thumb along the current, fingers curl with the field).

items.q: A square loop of side $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ carries $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$. What is the magnetic field at its centre?

A numerical sum confirms it.

items.q: Two identical coaxial circular loops of radius $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$, a distance $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ apart (Helmholtz arrangement), each carry $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in the same sense. What is the field at the point on the axis midway between them?
items.explain:
Each loop is $z=R/2=0.050\,\mathrm{m}$ from the midpoint: $B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0IR^2}{2(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.0)(0.010)}{2(0.0125)^{3/2}}=9.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}$.
Both point the same way: $B=2B_1=1.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ (and the field is remarkably uniform near the midpoint).

items.topic: Magnetic field of a straight wire
items.q: Two long parallel wires, $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart ($\pm5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the origin), carry $10\,\mathrm{A}$ in the same direction. What is the field magnitude at the point $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the midpoint on the perpendicular bisector?
items.explain:
Each wire is $\sqrt{0.05^2+0.12^2}=0.13\,\mathrm{m}$ from the point: $B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}=1.5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$, perpendicular to the line from the wire.
The components along the bisector cancel (the wires are symmetric); the components parallel to the line joining the wires add: $B=2B_1\dfrac{y}{r}=2(1.5\times10^{-5})\dfrac{0.12}{0.13}=2.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$ (equivalently $\dfrac{\mu_0Iy}{\pi(a^2+y^2)}$).

items.q: A proton moves at $3.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field it produces at a point $1.0\,\mathrm{nm}$ away, perpendicular to its velocity?

items.q: A rectangular loop of $0.20\,\mathrm{m}\times0.30\,\mathrm{m}$ is in a uniform field of $0.40\,\mathrm{T}$. The angle between the field and the loop's normal is $60^\circ$. What is the magnetic flux through the loop?
items.explain: $\Phi_B=BA\cos\theta=(0.40)(0.060)\cos60^\circ=1.2\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Wb}$ ($1\,\mathrm{Wb}=1\,\mathrm{T\,m^2}$), with $\theta$ measured from the normal.

items.q: A flat coil with $200$ turns and area $0.05\,\mathrm{m^2}$ is in a uniform field perpendicular to its plane. The field changes from $0$ to $1.5\,\mathrm{T}$ in $3.0\,\mathrm{s}$. What is the induced emf?
items.explain: Faraday: $|\varepsilon|=N\left|\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|=NA\dfrac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}=(200)(0.05)\dfrac{1.5}{3.0}=5.0\,\mathrm{V}$.

items.q: A square loop of side $2.00\,\mathrm{m}$ has half of its area in a uniform field perpendicular to it. The loop contains an ideal battery of emf $20.0\,\mathrm{V}$. The field varies as $B=0.0420-0.870\,t$ (T, s). If the induced emf has the same sense as the battery's, what is the net emf in the circuit?
items.explain:
Flux through the loop: $\Phi=B\cdot\dfrac{A_{\text{loop}}}{2}=B(2.00\,\mathrm{m^2})$, so $|\varepsilon_{\text{ind}}|=2.00\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|=2.00(0.870)=1.74\,\mathrm{V}$ (the field decreases, so the induced current tries to maintain the flux).
Net emf $=20.0+1.74=21.7\,\mathrm{V}$ (it would be $18.3\,\mathrm{V}$ if the induced emf opposed the battery).
items.src: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law of induction

items.q: A conducting rod of length $0.40\,\mathrm{m}$ slides at $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ perpendicular to a uniform $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$ field, along rails joined by a $2.0\,\Omega$ resistor. What force must be applied to keep the speed constant?
items.explain:
Motional emf $\varepsilon=BLv=(0.50)(0.40)(5.0)=1.0\,\mathrm{V}$; current $I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=0.50\,\mathrm{A}$.
Magnetic braking force $F=ILB=(0.50)(0.40)(0.50)=0.10\,\mathrm{N}$ - the applied force must match it, and supplies the power $Fv=\varepsilon I=0.50\,\mathrm{W}$ dissipated in the resistor.

items.q: A coil of $100$ turns and area $0.020\,\mathrm{m^2}$ rotates at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ in a uniform $0.20\,\mathrm{T}$ field. What is the peak emf?
items.explain: $\Phi=NBA\cos\omega t\Rightarrow\varepsilon=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t}=NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, peak $NBA\omega=100(0.20)(0.020)(2\pi\cdot50)=1.3\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{V}$. (Using $f$ instead of $\omega=2\pi f$ is a common slip.)
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law

items.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed TOWARDS a conducting loop (loop plane perpendicular to the magnet's axis). The induced current in the loop produces a magnetic field that
opts: points in the same direction as the magnet's field at the loop
has no effect on the magnet
items.explain: Lenz's law: the induced effect opposes the CHANGE (increasing flux of the north pole's field). The loop behaves as a north pole facing the magnet, repelling it; energy for the induced current comes from the work done pushing the magnet.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.2 (Lenz's law)

items.q: A uniform field points INTO the page and its magnitude is decreasing. The induced current in a circular loop in the plane of the page is
items.explain: The inward flux decreases, so the induced current produces an inward field of its own to oppose the decrease: by the right-hand rule a CLOCKWISE current gives a field into the page inside the loop.
items.src: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Lenz's law

items.q: Which change induces an emf in a closed loop?
opts: a steady current in the loop
any change of the magnetic flux through it: the field, the area or the orientation
items.explain: $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$ can change through $B$, $A$ or $\theta$; only $\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d}t\neq0$ gives an emf.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.2

items.q: A uniform field inside a long solenoid of radius $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ changes at $0.10\,\mathrm{T/s}$. What is the magnitude of the induced electric field at $0.04\,\mathrm{m}$ from the axis (inside)?
items.explain: $\oint\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t}$: $E(2\pi r)=\pi r^2\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\Rightarrow E=\dfrac r2\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|=\dfrac{0.04}{2}(0.10)=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{V/m}$ (circular field lines).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), induced electric field

items.q: For the same solenoid (radius $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$, $\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}t=0.10\,\mathrm{T/s}$), what is the induced field magnitude $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ from the axis (OUTSIDE the solenoid)?
items.explain: Outside, the flux is confined to $\pi R^2$: $E(2\pi r)=\pi R^2\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{R^2}{2r}\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|=\dfrac{0.010}{0.40}(0.10)=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{V/m}$: the field is NOT zero outside, although $B$ is.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), induced electric field

items.q: What is the inductance of an air-filled solenoid with $1000$ turns, cross-section $4.0\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ and length $0.25\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain: $L=\dfrac{N\Phi_B}{I}=\mu_0n^2Al=\dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{\ell}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(10^6)(4.0\times10^{-4})}{0.25}=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{H}$.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.5 (inductor and inductance)

items.q: The current through a $2.0\,\mathrm{mH}$ inductor changes at $50\,\mathrm{A/s}$. What is the magnitude of the self-induced emf?
items.explain: $|\varepsilon_L|=L\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|=(2.0\times10^{-3})(50)=0.10\,\mathrm{V}$, opposing the change of current (Lenz).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.6 (self-induction)

items.q: How much energy is stored in the magnetic field of a $2.0\,\mathrm{H}$ inductor carrying $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$?
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.5

items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.5

items.q: Two coils have mutual inductance $5.0\,\mathrm{mH}$. The current in coil 1 changes at $100\,\mathrm{A/s}$. What emf is induced in coil 2?
items.explain: $|\varepsilon_2|=M\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I_1}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|=(5.0\times10^{-3})(100)=0.50\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.6 (mutual induction)

items.q: A $12\,\mathrm{V}$ battery is connected at $t=0$ to a $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor in series with a $0.20\,\mathrm{H}$ inductor. What is the current after one time constant ($t=L/R$)?
items.explain:
$I(t)=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right)$ with $\tau=\dfrac LR=0.050\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\dfrac\varepsilon R=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$.
At $t=\tau$: $I=3.0(1-e^{-1})=1.9\,\mathrm{A}$, i.e. $63\%$ of the final value (numerical integration of $L\,\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t+RI=\varepsilon$ agrees).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26): beyond the chapter 7 outline (RL circuit)

items.q: An inductor opposes
opts: a change in the current through it
items.explain: $\varepsilon_L=-L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$ acts against the CHANGE; a steady current in an ideal inductor produces no emf.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.5-7.6

items.q: The SI unit of magnetic flux, the weber, is equal to
items.explain: $\Phi_B=BA$, so $1\,\mathrm{Wb}=1\,\mathrm{T\,m^2}=1\,\mathrm{V\,s}$ (since $\varepsilon=\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d}t$).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.1 (magnetic flux)

items.q: A uniform magnetic field out of the page through a circular loop in the plane of the page is increasing in magnitude. What is the direction of the induced current?
items.explain:
Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the CHANGE of flux. The flux out of is increasing, so the induced field must point into the page (it opposes an increasing outward flux).
By the right-hand rule the loop current that gives that field is clockwise.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Lenz's law

items.explain:

By the right-hand rule the loop current that gives that field is counter-clockwise.

items.q: A coil of $50$ turns and area $0.040\,\mathrm{m^2}$ is perpendicular to a field that varies as $B=0.50\,t^2$ (tesla, with $t$ in seconds). What is the induced emf at $t=2.0\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain: $\Phi=NBA=50(0.040)(0.50\,t^2)=1.0\,t^2$ (Wb), so $|\varepsilon|=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t}=2.0\,t=4.0\,\mathrm{V}$ at $t=2.0\,\mathrm{s}$ (not $\Phi/t$: the emf is the RATE of change).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law

items.q: An aircraft with a $40\,\mathrm{m}$ wingspan flies horizontally at $250\,\mathrm{m/s}$ through the vertical component of Earth's field, $5.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}$. What emf appears between the wingtips?
items.explain: The wing is a rod of length $L=40\,\mathrm{m}$ moving across the field: $\varepsilon=BLv=(5.0\times10^{-5})(40)(250)=0.50\,\mathrm{V}$ (not measurable with a voltmeter attached to the wingtips: it is just the other half of a circuit moving in the same field).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law

items.q: A circular loop in a uniform $0.40\,\mathrm{T}$ field (perpendicular to it) expands so that its radius grows at $2.0\,\mathrm{mm/s}$. What is the induced emf when $r=0.10\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain: $\Phi=B\pi r^2\Rightarrow\varepsilon=B\dfrac{\mathrm{d}(\pi r^2)}{\mathrm{d}t}=2\pi rB\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}=2\pi(0.10)(0.40)(0.0020)=5.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law

items.q: A loop of resistance $0.50\,\Omega$ has an induced emf of $0.10\,\mathrm{V}$. What current flows?
items.explain: $I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=\dfrac{0.10}{0.50}=0.20\,\mathrm{A}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law

items.q: A coil of $200$ turns carries $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, producing a flux of $5.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Wb}$ through each turn. What is its inductance?
items.explain: $L=\dfrac{N\Phi_B}{I}=\dfrac{(200)(5.0\times10^{-4})}{2.0}=0.050\,\mathrm{H}$ (the flux LINKAGE $N\Phi_B$, not the flux of one turn).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.5

items.q: An inductor shows a self-induced emf of $0.30\,\mathrm{V}$ when the current changes at $15\,\mathrm{A/s}$. What is its inductance?
items.explain: $L=\dfrac{|\varepsilon_L|}{|\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t|}=\dfrac{0.30}{15}=0.020\,\mathrm{H}$.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.6

items.q: A metal rod moves through a uniform magnetic field with its velocity parallel to the field lines. The motional emf along the rod is
items.explain: $\varepsilon=\oint(\vec v\times\vec B)\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec l=0$ when $\vec v\parallel\vec B$: the magnetic force on the charges vanishes.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.2

items.q: Lenz's law is a statement of conservation of
items.explain: If the induced current aided the change that causes it, the effect would feed itself and energy would be created from nothing; the opposition means mechanical work must be done to induce the current.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.2

items.q: An electric field induced by a changing magnetic field has field lines that
opts: start on positive charges and end on negative charges
form closed loops (it is not conservative)
items.explain: Faraday's law: $\oint\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t}\neq0$, so $\vec E$ circulates: the induced field is non-conservative and potential is not defined for it.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.4

items.q: A coil is rotated at constant angular speed in a uniform magnetic field. The induced emf is
items.explain: $\Phi=NBA\cos\omega t$, so $\varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin\omega t$ - the principle of the AC generator.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.2

items.q: An RL circuit has $R=4.0\,\Omega$ and $L=0.20\,\mathrm{H}$. What is its time constant?
items.explain: $\tau=\dfrac LR=\dfrac{0.20}{4.0}=0.050\,\mathrm{s}$: after $\tau$ the current has reached $63\%$ of its final value.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26): beyond the chapter 7 outline (RL circuit)

items.q: A circular loop of radius $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ is in a uniform $0.60\,\mathrm{T}$ field. The loop's normal makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the field. What is the flux through the loop?
items.explain: $\Phi_B=B\,\pi r^2\cos\theta=(0.60)\pi(0.050)^2\cos30^\circ=4.1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.1

items.q: The flux of a uniform field through a loop is zero when
opts: the plane of the loop is parallel to the field
the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field
items.explain: $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$ is zero for $\theta=90^\circ$, i.e. when the normal is perpendicular to $\vec B$ (the loop edge-on to the field lines).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.1

items.q: The magnetic flux through each turn of a $50$-turn coil falls uniformly from $0.040\,\mathrm{Wb}$ to zero in $0.020\,\mathrm{s}$. What is the induced emf?
items.explain: $|\varepsilon|=N\left|\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|=50\times\dfrac{0.040}{0.020}=100\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law

items.q: A single loop of area $0.010\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and resistance $0.10\,\Omega$ is perpendicular to a field changing at $0.50\,\mathrm{T/s}$. What current is induced?
items.explain: $\varepsilon=A\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|=(0.010)(0.50)=5.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{V}$; $I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}=\dfrac{5.0\times10^{-3}}{0.10}=0.050\,\mathrm{A}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Final tutoring slides 2025-26 (induction), Faraday's law

items.q: A coil of $50$ turns is wound tightly around the middle of a long solenoid ($1000$ turns, length $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$, cross-section $2.0\,\mathrm{cm^2}$). What is their mutual inductance?
items.explain: A current $I_1$ in the solenoid gives $B=\mu_0\dfrac{N_1}{\ell}I_1$ and a flux $BA$ through each turn of the small coil: $M=\dfrac{N_2\Phi_{21}}{I_1}=\dfrac{\mu_0N_1N_2A}{\ell}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1000)(50)(2.0\times10^{-4})}{0.20}=6.3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{H}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.6

items.q: The henry (H) is equal to
items.explain: $L=\dfrac{N\Phi_B}{I}$ gives Wb/A, and $\varepsilon=L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$ gives V s/A.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.5

items.q: A magnet falls through a long vertical copper tube and takes much longer than a non-magnetic object. The explanation is
opts: eddy currents induced in the tube oppose the magnet's motion
air resistance is greater inside a tube
the magnet is attracted to the copper
items.explain: Lenz's law: the changing flux induces currents in the tube whose fields oppose the magnet's motion (a magnetic braking force). Copper is not magnetic and the magnet is not attracted to it.
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.2 (Lenz's law)

items.q: In a circuit carrying a STEADY direct current, an ideal inductor behaves like
opts: a plain wire (no voltage across it)
items.explain: $\varepsilon_L=-L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$ for constant $I$; the inductor only resists CHANGES of current (it stores the energy $\tfrac12LI^2$).
items.src: Magnetism lecture (2025-26), chapter 7, 7.5-7.6

items.q: A single square loop of side $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ rotates at $120\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ about a diameter in a $0.30\,\mathrm{T}$ field. What is the peak emf?
items.explain: $\varepsilon_{\max}=NBA\omega=1(0.30)(0.040)(120)=1.4\,\mathrm{V}$.

items.q: Two plane mirrors meet at right angles. A laser beam strikes the first at a point $11.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the intersection and, after reflecting, hits the midpoint of the second mirror ($28.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ long). What is the angle of incidence at the first mirror?
items.explain:
The reflected ray goes from $(11.5,\,0)$ on the first mirror to $(0,\,14.0)$ on the second: it makes an angle $\theta$ with the NORMAL of the first mirror where $\tan\theta=\dfrac{11.5}{14.0}$.
$\theta=\arctan0.821=39.4^\circ$. By the law of reflection this is also the angle of incidence.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.1

items.q: Visible light of wavelength $380\,\mathrm{nm}$ (violet, measured in air) enters the vitreous humor of the eye, $n=1.34$. What is its wavelength inside?
items.explain: The frequency stays the same; the wavelength shrinks by $n$: $\lambda=\dfrac{\lambda_0}{n}=\dfrac{380}{1.34}=284\,\mathrm{nm}$ (the red end, $750\,\mathrm{nm}$, becomes $560\,\mathrm{nm}$).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.2(a)

items.q: What is the frequency of red light of wavelength $750\,\mathrm{nm}$ (in air), and does it change inside the humor ($n=1.34$)?
items.explain: $f=\dfrac{c}{\lambda_0}=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{750\times10^{-9}}=4.00\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and it is the SAME inside the humor: the frequency is set by the source; speed and wavelength both change.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.2(b)

items.q: What is the speed of light inside the vitreous humor ($n=1.34$)?
items.explain: $v=\dfrac cn=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{1.34}=2.24\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.2(c)

items.q: A parallel beam of light in air makes an angle of $47.5^\circ$ with the SURFACE of a glass plate of refractive index $1.66$. What is the angle between the refracted beam and the surface?
items.explain:
Angles in Snell's law are measured from the NORMAL: $\theta_1=90^\circ-47.5^\circ=42.5^\circ$.
$\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{\sin42.5^\circ}{1.66}=0.407\Rightarrow\theta_2=24.0^\circ$ from the normal, i.e. $66.0^\circ$ from the surface. (Fermat's principle - minimising the travel time numerically - gives the same bend.)
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.7(b)

items.q: A beam in air makes an angle of $47.5^\circ$ with the surface of a glass plate. What is the angle between the REFLECTED beam and the surface?
items.explain: Law of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, whether both are measured from the normal ($42.5^\circ$) or both from the surface ($47.5^\circ$).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.7(a)

items.q: The critical angle for total internal reflection at a liquid-air interface is $42.5^\circ$. What is the refractive index of the liquid?
items.explain: At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface ($90^\circ$): $n\sin\theta_c=1\Rightarrow n=\dfrac{1}{\sin42.5^\circ}=1.48$.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.17

items.q: The liquid ($n=1.48$, critical angle $42.5^\circ$) lies below air. A ray in the liquid reaches the surface at $35.0^\circ$. At what angle to the normal does it emerge into the air?
items.explain: $n_{liq}\sin35.0^\circ=\sin\theta\Rightarrow\sin\theta=1.48\times0.574=0.849\Rightarrow\theta=58.1^\circ$: the ray bends AWAY from the normal going into the less dense medium (and $35.0^\circ<42.5^\circ$, so it does emerge).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.17(a)

items.q: For the same liquid ($n=1.48$), a ray in AIR hits the surface at $35.0^\circ$ to the normal. What is the angle of refraction in the liquid?
items.explain: $\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{\sin35.0^\circ}{1.48}=0.388\Rightarrow\theta_2=22.8^\circ$: towards the normal when entering the denser medium.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.17(b)

items.q: A beam hits glass at $57.0^\circ$ to the normal in air. Red light refracts at $38.1^\circ$ and violet at $36.7^\circ$. What is the refractive index of the glass for red light?
items.explain: Snell: $n_r=\dfrac{\sin57.0^\circ}{\sin38.1^\circ}=\dfrac{0.8387}{0.6173}=1.36$ (violet: $\dfrac{0.8387}{0.5976}=1.40$ - violet bends more).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.25(a)

items.q: In that glass the index is $1.36$ for red and $1.40$ for violet. What is the speed of VIOLET light in the glass?
items.explain: $v=\dfrac cn=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{1.40}=2.14\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, slower than red ($2.21\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$): the glass disperses white light.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.25(b)

items.q: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through two polarising filters. The first axis is $60.0^\circ$ from the vertical; the second axis is horizontal. What fraction of $I_0$ emerges?
items.explain:
The first filter halves the intensity: $I_1=\tfrac12I_0$. The angle between the axes is $90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ$.
Malus' law: $I_2=I_1\cos^2\theta=\tfrac12I_0\cos^230^\circ=0.375\,I_0$.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.27

items.q: Unpolarised light in air is incident at $54.5^\circ$ on a plane glass surface and the reflected beam is completely linearly polarised. What is the refractive index of the glass?
items.explain: Brewster's law: $\tan\theta_B=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\Rightarrow n=\tan54.5^\circ=1.40$.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.31(a)

items.q: For that glass ($n=1.40$) at the Brewster angle $54.5^\circ$, what is the angle of refraction of the transmitted beam?
items.explain: At the Brewster angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so $\theta_r=90^\circ-\theta_B=35.5^\circ$ (check with Snell: $\sin35.5^\circ=\dfrac{\sin54.5^\circ}{1.40}$).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.31(b)

items.q: What is Brewster's angle for light in air reflecting from crown glass ($n=1.5$)?
items.explain: $\tan\theta_B=n=1.5\Rightarrow\theta_B=56.3^\circ$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.31

items.q: What is Brewster's angle for light in air reflecting from water ($n=1.33$)?
items.explain: $\tan\theta_B=n=1.33\Rightarrow\theta_B=53.1^\circ$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.31

items.q: Linearly polarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through a polariser whose axis makes 30° with the plane of polarisation. What is the transmitted intensity (in units of $I_0$)?
items.explain: Malus' law: $I=I_0\cos^2\theta=\cos^230^\circ=0.75\,I_0$ (the amplitude is multiplied by $\cos\theta$, the intensity by $\cos^2\theta$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.27

items.q: Linearly polarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through a polariser whose axis makes 60° with the plane of polarisation. What is the transmitted intensity (in units of $I_0$)?
items.explain: Malus' law: $I=I_0\cos^2\theta=\cos^260^\circ=0.25\,I_0$ (the amplitude is multiplied by $\cos\theta$, the intensity by $\cos^2\theta$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.27

items.q: Linearly polarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through a polariser whose axis makes 20° with the plane of polarisation. What is the transmitted intensity (in units of $I_0$)?
items.explain: Malus' law: $I=I_0\cos^2\theta=\cos^220^\circ=0.883\,I_0$ (the amplitude is multiplied by $\cos\theta$, the intensity by $\cos^2\theta$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.27

items.q: Ultrasound travels at $344\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in the lungs and $1480\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in muscle. A beam leaves the lungs at $9.73^\circ$ from the normal to the heart wall. At what angle from the normal does it enter the heart? (Snell's law applies with $n=v_{air}/v$.)
items.explain:
Define $n_{lung}=\dfrac{344}{344}=1$ and $n_{muscle}=\dfrac{344}{1480}=0.232$. Snell: $\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{n_1}{n_2}\sin\theta_1=\dfrac{1480}{344}\sin9.73^\circ=0.727$.
$\theta_2=46.6^\circ$: the sound bends AWAY from the normal into the faster medium.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.37(a)

items.q: For sound waves going from air ($344\,\mathrm{m/s}$) into muscle ($1480\,\mathrm{m/s}$), what is the critical angle?
items.explain: Total reflection occurs when the transmitted ray would exceed $90^\circ$: $\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{v_{air}}{v_{muscle}}=\dfrac{344}{1480}=0.232\Rightarrow\theta_c=13.4^\circ$ (waves entering the faster medium).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.37(b)

items.q: A ray in a glass block ($n=1.52$) reaches the top surface at $57.2^\circ$ to the normal. When a layer of oil is placed on the glass the ray is totally reflected. What is the maximum possible refractive index of the oil?
items.explain:
Total reflection at the glass-oil interface needs the incidence angle $\ge$ the critical angle: $n_g\sin57.2^\circ\ge n_{oil}$.
$n_{oil,\max}=1.52\sin57.2^\circ=1.28$ (a denser oil, $n>1.28$, would let the ray through).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.41

items.q: What is the critical angle for light going from glass ($n=1.52$) into air?
items.explain: $\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{1}{n}=\dfrac1{1.52}\Rightarrow\theta_c=41.1^\circ$ (the larger $n$, the smaller $\theta_c$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.17

items.q: What is the critical angle for light going from water ($n=1.33$) into air?
items.explain: $\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{1}{n}=\dfrac1{1.33}\Rightarrow\theta_c=48.8^\circ$ (the larger $n$, the smaller $\theta_c$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.17

items.q: What is the critical angle for light going from diamond ($n=2.42$) into air?
items.explain: $\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{1}{n}=\dfrac1{2.42}\Rightarrow\theta_c=24.4^\circ$ (the larger $n$, the smaller $\theta_c$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.17

items.q: A ray in air hits a water surface ($n=1.33$) at $40^\circ$ to the normal. At what angle to the normal does it travel in the water?
items.explain: $n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2\Rightarrow\sin\theta_2=\dfrac{\sin40^\circ}{1.33}=0.483\Rightarrow\theta_2=28.9^\circ$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.7

items.q: Green light of wavelength $550\,\mathrm{nm}$ in air enters glass of refractive index $1.5$. What is its wavelength in the glass?
items.explain: $\lambda=\dfrac{\lambda_0}{n}=\dfrac{550}{1.5}=367\,\mathrm{nm}$; the colour (frequency) does not change.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.2

items.q: Rayleigh scattering is proportional to $1/\lambda^4$. How many times more strongly is violet light ($400\,\mathrm{nm}$) scattered than green light ($550\,\mathrm{nm}$)?
items.explain: $\dfrac{I_v}{I_g}=\left(\dfrac{\lambda_g}{\lambda_v}\right)^4=\left(\dfrac{550}{400}\right)^4=3.6$: short wavelengths scatter more, hence the blue sky (and red sunsets).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.35

items.q: A radio station broadcasts at $88.9\,\mathrm{MHz}$. What is the wavelength of its radio waves?
items.explain: $\lambda=\dfrac cf=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{88.9\times10^6}=3.37\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 36, 36.15

items.q: A plane electromagnetic wave has an electric-field amplitude of $100\,\mathrm{V/m}$. What is its intensity?
items.explain: $I=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0cE_{\max}^2=\tfrac12(8.85\times10^{-12})(3.00\times10^8)(100)^2=13\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$ (the average of $\varepsilon_0cE^2$ over a cycle gives the factor $\tfrac12$).
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (electromagnetic waves)

items.q: When light passes from air into glass, which quantity does NOT change?
items.explain: The frequency is fixed by the source. $v=c/n$ decreases and $\lambda=\lambda_0/n$ shrinks; the direction changes unless the incidence is normal.
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (refraction)

items.q: A plane mirror is turned through an angle $\alpha$ about an axis in its surface while the incident ray stays fixed. The reflected ray turns through
items.explain: The normal turns by $\alpha$, so the angle of incidence changes by $\alpha$, and the angle between incident and reflected rays changes by $2\alpha$.
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (reflection)

items.q: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels
opts: from lower to higher refractive index
from a medium of higher refractive index to one of lower index, at an angle above the critical angle
items.explain: Only going from a denser to a rarer medium is there a critical angle $\theta_c=\arcsin(n_2/n_1)$; this is the principle of optical fibres.
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (total internal reflection)

items.q: Which phenomenon shows that light is a TRANSVERSE wave?
items.explain: Only transverse waves can be polarised: the filter selects one direction of oscillation of $\vec E$. Reflection, refraction and diffraction occur for longitudinal waves (sound) too.
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (polarization)

items.q: In a vacuum, all electromagnetic waves (radio, visible light, X-rays) share the same
items.explain: $c=f\lambda$ is the same for all of them; frequency and wavelength vary inversely.
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (electromagnetic waves)

items.q: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index $1.50$ and cladding of index $1.45$. What is the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary?
items.explain: Light in the core is totally reflected at the cladding when $\sin\theta\ge\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$: $\theta_c=\arcsin\dfrac{1.45}{1.50}=75.2^\circ$ (measured from the normal to the boundary).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.17

items.q: For that fibre (core $1.50$, cladding $1.45$), what is the numerical aperture $\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}$ that fixes the largest acceptance angle from air?
items.explain: $\mathrm{NA}=\sqrt{1.50^2-1.45^2}=\sqrt{0.1475}=0.384$, so rays entering within $\arcsin0.384=22.6^\circ$ of the axis are guided.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.41

items.q: How long does light take to cross a glass slab ($n=1.5$) that is $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ thick?
items.explain: In glass the speed is $\dfrac cn=2.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $t=\dfrac{nL}{c}=\dfrac{(1.5)(0.020)}{3.00\times10^8}=1.0\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{s}$ ($nL$ is the optical path length).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.2

items.q: Light has a wavelength of $400\,\mathrm{nm}$ INSIDE water ($n=1.33$). What is its frequency?
items.explain: $f=\dfrac{v}{\lambda}=\dfrac{c/n}{\lambda}=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{(1.33)(400\times10^{-9})}=5.6\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (not $c/\lambda$: the $400\,\mathrm{nm}$ is the wavelength in water).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.2

items.q: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through three polarisers with axes at $0^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ to the vertical. What fraction of $I_0$ emerges?
items.explain: First: $\tfrac12I_0$. Second ($45^\circ$ between axes): $\times\cos^245^\circ=\tfrac12$. Third ($45^\circ$ again): $\times\tfrac12$. Total $I_0/8=0.125\,I_0$. Without the middle polariser the crossed pair would pass nothing.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.27

items.q: A $100\,\mathrm{W}$ point source radiates light uniformly in all directions. What is the intensity $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ away?
items.explain: $I=\dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}=\dfrac{100}{4\pi(2.0)^2}=2.0\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$ (inverse-square law).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (electromagnetic waves)

items.q: Light travels at $2.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a transparent material. What is its refractive index?
items.explain: $n=\dfrac cv=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{2.0\times10^8}=1.5$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 33, 33.25

items.q: Light passes from air into glass. In the glass the ray
items.explain: Entering a medium of higher index the speed decreases and the ray bends TOWARDS the normal ($\theta_2<\theta_1$).
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (refraction)

items.q: Why is the sky blue and the setting Sun red?
opts: the atmosphere reflects blue light from the sea
short wavelengths are scattered more strongly by air molecules ($\propto1/\lambda^4$)
items.explain: Rayleigh scattering removes blue from the direct beam (leaving it red at sunset) and sends it in all directions (blue sky).
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (scattering)

items.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at $30^\circ$ to the NORMAL. The angle between the incident and the reflected rays is
items.explain: The reflected ray is also $30^\circ$ from the normal, on the other side: $30^\circ+30^\circ=60^\circ$ between the rays.
items.src: Optics lecture: the nature and propagation of light (reflection)

items.q: A $9.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ pencil is held perpendicular to a plane mirror with the lead tip $12.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the mirror and the eraser end $21.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from it. What is the length of the image of the pencil?
items.explain: A plane mirror forms an image as far behind it as the object is in front, with $m=+1$: the image is $9.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ long, from $12.0$ to $21.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ behind the mirror (so the tip's image is the end nearer the mirror).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.3

items.q: An object $0.600\,\mathrm{cm}$ tall is $16.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ in front of a concave spherical mirror of radius of curvature $22.0\,\mathrm{cm}$. Where is the image (distance in front of the mirror)?
items.explain: $f=\dfrac R2=11.0\,\mathrm{cm}$. Mirror equation $\dfrac1s+\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f$: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1{11.0}-\dfrac1{16.5}=\dfrac{1}{33.0}\Rightarrow s'=33.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ in front of the mirror (real). An ABCD ray-matrix calculation gives the same position.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.5(b)

items.q: For the same concave mirror ($f=11.0\,\mathrm{cm}$) and object ($0.600\,\mathrm{cm}$ tall, $16.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ away), what is the height of the image, and is it erect or inverted? (Give the signed height; negative = inverted.)
items.explain: $m=-\dfrac{s'}{s}=-\dfrac{33.0}{16.5}=-2.00$: INVERTED and twice as large. $h'=mh=-1.20\,\mathrm{cm}$. The image is real (in front of the mirror, $s'>0$).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.5(b)

items.q: A convex mirror has a radius of curvature of $3.00\,\mathrm{cm}$. An object is $18.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ in front of it. Where is the image? (Negative: behind the mirror.)
items.explain:
A convex mirror has a NEGATIVE focal length: $f=-\dfrac R2=-1.50\,\mathrm{cm}$.
$\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1s=-\dfrac1{1.50}-\dfrac1{18.0}=-0.722\Rightarrow s'=-1.38\,\mathrm{cm}$: virtual, behind the mirror.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.8

items.q: For that convex mirror ($f=-1.50\,\mathrm{cm}$) and an object $18.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ away, what is the lateral magnification?
items.explain: $m=-\dfrac{s'}{s}=-\dfrac{-1.385}{18.0}=+0.0769$: erect and much smaller (a convex mirror always gives a diminished, upright, virtual image).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.8

items.q: A dentist wants an ERECT image with magnification $2.00$ when the mirror is $1.25\,\mathrm{cm}$ from a tooth. What focal length is needed (positive for a concave mirror)?
items.explain:
Erect and magnified means a virtual image: $s'=-ms=-2.50\,\mathrm{cm}$.
$\dfrac1f=\dfrac1s+\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1{1.25}-\dfrac1{2.50}=0.40\Rightarrow f=+2.50\,\mathrm{cm}$: a CONCAVE mirror with $R=5.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ (the object lies inside the focal length).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.13

items.q: A speck of dirt is embedded $3.50\,\mathrm{cm}$ below the surface of a sheet of ice ($n=1.309$). What is its apparent depth when viewed from directly above?
items.explain: Plane refracting surface, viewed along the normal: $d_{app}=d\,\dfrac{n_{air}}{n_{ice}}=\dfrac{3.50}{1.309}=2.67\,\mathrm{cm}$ (objects under water or ice look closer to the surface).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.19

items.q: A swimmer $0.80\,\mathrm{m}$ below the surface of a pool ($n=1.33$) sees the diving board directly overhead at an apparent height of $5.20\,\mathrm{m}$ ABOVE HER. What is the actual height of the board above the water?
items.explain:
The image is $5.20\,\mathrm{m}$ above the swimmer, i.e. $5.20-0.80=4.40\,\mathrm{m}$ above the SURFACE.
Object in air seen from water: $h_{app}=\dfrac{n_{water}}{n_{air}}h\Rightarrow h=\dfrac{4.40}{1.33}=3.31\,\mathrm{m}$ (things above the surface look higher to a swimmer).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.21

items.q: The end of a long glass rod ($n=1.60$) is ground to a convex hemispherical surface of radius $4.00\,\mathrm{cm}$. An object is on the axis $24.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ in front of the vertex. Where is the image (inside the glass, measured from the vertex)?
items.explain:
Refraction at a spherical surface: $\dfrac{n_a}{s}+\dfrac{n_b}{s'}=\dfrac{n_b-n_a}{R}$ with $n_a=1$, $n_b=1.60$, $R=+4.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ (centre on the outgoing side).
$\dfrac{1}{24.0}+\dfrac{1.60}{s'}=0.150\Rightarrow\dfrac{1.60}{s'}=0.1083\Rightarrow s'=14.8\,\mathrm{cm}$ (real, in the glass). A ray-matrix calculation agrees.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.26

items.q: For that rod (object $24.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ away, image at $14.8\,\mathrm{cm}$ inside the glass), the arrow is $1.50\,\mathrm{mm}$ tall. What is the (signed) height of the image?
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.26

items.q: A thin planoconvex lens (flat face on the left, curved face of radius $13.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ on the right, $n=1.70$) is made. What is its focal length?
items.explain: Lensmaker's formula: $\dfrac1f=(n-1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}\right)$ with $R_1=\infty$ and $R_2=-13.0\,\mathrm{cm}$: $\dfrac1f=0.70\left(\dfrac1{13.0}\right)\Rightarrow f=18.6\,\mathrm{cm}$ (converging).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29

items.q: An insect $3.75\,\mathrm{mm}$ tall is $22.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the left of a thin converging lens of focal length $18.6\,\mathrm{cm}$. Where is the image (to the right of the lens)?
items.explain: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1s=\dfrac1{18.57}-\dfrac1{22.5}=9.40\times10^{-3}\Rightarrow s'=106\,\mathrm{cm}$ (real). The magnification is $m=-\dfrac{s'}{s}=-4.73$, so the image is $17.7\,\mathrm{mm}$ tall and inverted.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29(a)

items.q: For that insect ($3.75\,\mathrm{mm}$ tall, $22.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ from a lens with $f=18.57\,\mathrm{cm}$), what is the signed height of the image in mm?
items.explain: $m=-\dfrac{s'}{s}=-\dfrac{106.4}{22.5}=-4.73$, $h'=-4.73(3.75)=-17.7\,\mathrm{mm}$: real, inverted, magnified.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29(a)

items.q: If the planoconvex lens is turned around (curved face towards the insect), the focal length of the (thin) lens and the image position
opts: do not change: $f$ depends only on $n$ and the two radii
items.explain: $\dfrac1f=(n-1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}\right)$ gives the same $f$ for both orientations of a thin lens (reversing swaps $R_1\to-R_2$ and $R_2\to-R_1$).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29(b)

items.q: A converging lens of focal length $70.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ forms an image $4.50\,\mathrm{cm}$ tall, inverted, of a real object $3.20\,\mathrm{cm}$ tall. How far is the object from the lens?
items.explain:
Inverted real image: $m=-\dfrac{4.50}{3.20}=-1.406=-\dfrac{s'}{s}\Rightarrow s'=1.406\,s$.
$\dfrac1s+\dfrac1{1.406s}=\dfrac1{70.0}\Rightarrow\dfrac{1.711}{s}=\dfrac{1}{70.0}\Rightarrow s=120\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $s'=168\,\mathrm{cm}$ (real).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.32

items.q: For that lens ($f=70.0\,\mathrm{cm}$, object at $120\,\mathrm{cm}$ giving $m=-1.406$), how far from the lens is the image?
items.explain: $s'=-ms=1.406\times119.8=168\,\mathrm{cm}$ on the other side (real); check: $\dfrac1{119.8}+\dfrac1{168.4}=\dfrac1{70.0}$.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.32

items.q: A $1.20\,\mathrm{cm}$ tall object is $50.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the left of a converging lens ($f=40.0\,\mathrm{cm}$). A second converging lens ($f=60.0\,\mathrm{cm}$) is $300.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the right of the first. Where is the image formed by the FIRST lens (to its right)?
items.explain: $\dfrac1{s_1'}=\dfrac1{40.0}-\dfrac1{50.0}=\dfrac1{200}\Rightarrow s_1'=200\,\mathrm{cm}$, $m_1=-4.00$: a real, inverted image $4.80\,\mathrm{cm}$ tall.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.43(a)

items.q: In the two-lens system above, the first image ($200\,\mathrm{cm}$ from lens 1) is the object for lens 2 ($f=60.0\,\mathrm{cm}$, $300.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from lens 1). Where is the FINAL image (to the right of lens 2)?
items.explain:
Object distance for lens 2: $s_2=300-200=100\,\mathrm{cm}$ (real object).
$\dfrac1{s_2'}=\dfrac1{60.0}-\dfrac1{100}\Rightarrow s_2'=150\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the right of lens 2 (checked by multiplying the two ray-transfer matrices).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.43(b)

items.q: For the same system, what is the signed height of the final image (negative means inverted compared with the object)?
items.explain:
$m_1=-4.00$ and $m_2=-\dfrac{150}{100}=-1.50$. Total magnification $m=m_1m_2=+6.00$.
Final image height $=6.00(1.20)=7.20\,\mathrm{cm}$, ERECT relative to the object (two inversions).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.43(b)

items.q: Two thin lenses of focal length magnitude $12.0\,\mathrm{cm}$, the first diverging and the second converging, are $9.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart. An object $2.50\,\mathrm{mm}$ tall is $20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the left of the diverging lens. How far from the FIRST lens is the final image?
items.explain:
Lens 1 ($f=-12.0$): $\dfrac1{s_1'}=-\dfrac1{12}-\dfrac1{20}\Rightarrow s_1'=-7.50\,\mathrm{cm}$ (virtual, on the object side).
Lens 2: object distance $s_2=9.00+7.50=16.5\,\mathrm{cm}$; $\dfrac1{s_2'}=\dfrac1{12}-\dfrac1{16.5}\Rightarrow s_2'=44.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ to the right of lens 2, i.e. $53.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from lens 1. The final image is real.
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.45(a, b)

items.q: For that two-lens system (diverging $f=-12.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ then converging $f=+12.0\,\mathrm{cm}$, $9.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart, object $2.50\,\mathrm{mm}$ tall at $20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$), what is the signed height of the final image in mm?
items.explain:
$m_1=-\dfrac{s_1'}{s_1}=-\dfrac{-7.50}{20.0}=+0.375$ and $m_2=-\dfrac{44.0}{16.5}=-2.67$; $m=m_1m_2=-1.00$.
The final image is $2.50\,\mathrm{mm}$ tall and INVERTED (negative height).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.45(c)

items.q: A slide projector must put a sharp image of a slide on a screen $9.00\,\mathrm{m}$ from the lens when the slide is $15.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the lens. What focal length is required?
items.explain: $\dfrac1f=\dfrac1s+\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1{15.0}+\dfrac1{900}\Rightarrow f=14.75\,\mathrm{cm}$ (just a little shorter than the slide distance: the slide sits just inside $2f$... just outside $f$).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.50(a)

items.q: The projector above has the slide $15.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ and the screen $9.00\,\mathrm{m}$ from the lens. A $24\,\mathrm{mm}\times36\,\mathrm{mm}$ slide fills a screen of width
items.explain: $|m|=\dfrac{s'}{s}=\dfrac{900}{15.0}=60$: the $36\,\mathrm{mm}$ side becomes $2.16\,\mathrm{m}$ and the $24\,\mathrm{mm}$ side $1.44\,\mathrm{m}$ (the image is inverted).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.50(b)

items.q: A simple magnifier has focal length $8.00\,\mathrm{cm}$. How far in front of it must an object be placed so that the image is formed at the observer's near point, $25.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ in front of the lens?
items.explain: The image is virtual, on the object's side: $s'=-25.0\,\mathrm{cm}$. $\dfrac1s=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1{8.00}+\dfrac1{25.0}=0.165\Rightarrow s=6.06\,\mathrm{cm}$ (inside the focal length).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.59(a)

items.q: For that magnifier ($f=8.00\,\mathrm{cm}$, image at the near point, object at $6.06\,\mathrm{cm}$), a $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ high object gives an image of what height?
items.explain: $m=-\dfrac{s'}{s}=\dfrac{25.0}{6.06}=4.13$ (erect, virtual): the image is $4.13\,\mathrm{mm}$ high ($m=1+\dfrac{25}{f}=4.13$ when the image is at the near point).
items.src: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.59(b)

items.q: An object is 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image (positive: on the far side, real; negative: same side as the object, virtual)?
items.explain: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1s=\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{30}\Rightarrow s'=15\,\mathrm{cm}$, so the image is real and inverted (magnification $m=-s'/s=-0.5$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29-34.45

items.q: An object is 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image (positive: on the far side, real; negative: same side as the object, virtual)?
items.explain: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1s=\dfrac1{20}-\dfrac1{15}\Rightarrow s'=-60\,\mathrm{cm}$, so the image is virtual and erect (magnification $m=-s'/s=4$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29-34.45

items.q: An object is 30 cm from a diverging lens of focal length -15 cm. Where is the image (positive: on the far side, real; negative: same side as the object, virtual)?
items.explain: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1s=\dfrac1{-15}-\dfrac1{30}\Rightarrow s'=-10\,\mathrm{cm}$, so the image is virtual and erect (magnification $m=-s'/s=0.333$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29-34.45

items.q: A biconvex lens has radii of curvature $R_1=+20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $R_2=-20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ and refractive index $1.50$. What is its focal length?
items.explain: $\dfrac1f=(n-1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}\right)=0.50\left(\dfrac1{20}+\dfrac1{20}\right)=\dfrac1{20}\Rightarrow f=20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.29-34.31

items.q: A lens has a focal length of $25\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is its power in dioptres?
items.explain: $P=\dfrac1f=\dfrac{1}{0.25\,\mathrm{m}}=4.0\,\mathrm{D}$ (focal length in metres).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.59

items.q: A fish is $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ below the surface of a pond ($n=1.33$). How deep does it appear to an observer looking straight down?
items.explain: $d_{app}=\dfrac{d}{n}=\dfrac{2.0}{1.33}=1.5\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.19

items.q: A person stands $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ in front of a plane mirror. How far is she from her image?
items.explain: The image is $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ behind the mirror, so the distance between her and the image is $2.0+2.0=4.0\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.3

items.q: An object is placed INSIDE the focal length of a converging lens. The image is
items.explain: For $s<f$: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1s<0$, so $s'<0$ (virtual, same side as the object) and $m=-\dfrac{s'}{s}>1$: the magnifying-glass arrangement.
items.src: Optics lecture: geometric optics (thin lenses)

items.q: A convex mirror always forms an image that is
items.explain: With $f<0$: $s'=\dfrac{sf}{s-f}$ is negative with $|s'|<s$, so $m=-s'/s$ is between $0$ and $1$.
items.src: Optics lecture: geometric optics (spherical mirrors)

items.q: A converging lens has a focal length of $15\,\mathrm{cm}$. Parallel rays from a distant object are focused
items.explain: For $s\to\infty$: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f\Rightarrow s'=f$: the focal point.
items.src: Optics lecture: geometric optics (thin lenses)

items.q: In the lens equation $\frac1s+\frac1{s'}=\frac1f$ a NEGATIVE image distance $s'$ means the image is
opts: virtual, on the same side of the lens as the object
items.explain: Sign convention: $s'>0$ for a real image on the outgoing side; $s'<0$ for a virtual image on the incoming side.
items.src: Optics lecture: geometric optics (sign conventions)

items.q: An object is $10.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ from a concave mirror of focal length $20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ (inside the focal point). Where is the image (negative: behind the mirror)?
items.explain: $\dfrac1{s'}=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1s=\dfrac1{20}-\dfrac1{10}=-\dfrac1{20}\Rightarrow s'=-20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$: a virtual image behind the mirror, with $m=-\dfrac{s'}{s}=+2.0$ (erect, magnified: a make-up mirror).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Tutorial chapter 34, 34.5
